utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I understand there is a point that you wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A very short point. It seems it's probably our duty for one reason or another but a little hard to decide precisely on which ground to ensure that the accused is aware of a rather odd coincidence of events that happened yesterday before he concludes his dealings with the present witness. The Court may not know this, alternatively it may have already heard it from other sources, but the person Dragan Jasovic, who is one of the -- one of the officials who took the statements that are, amongst other issues, in issue with this witness - so for example, he's the named officer in tab 52, the statement of Afrim Mustafa - was giving evidence yesterday in this court and indeed in this very room, called by the Prosecution in the Limaj case. Not known to us in advance, he's been giving evidence, I think, on Monday and Tuesday. He's still in the building, still in the town and will be in the building again this afternoon, his cross-examination at the hands of one defendant having concluded and cross-examination being set to continue this afternoon. So there it is. He is a person who has been called by the Prosecution in another case, and he happens to be here in town at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks for the information, Mr. Nice. Let the witness be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you may continue with your cross-examination. Sorry. Mr. Milosevic to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. In relation to the information just provided by Mr. Nice that Mr. Jasovic, who is one of the authorised officials appearing in tab 52, as he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, had you wished to comment on the matter, I would have thought you would have commented on it before. Nonetheless, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if there's any controversy with regard to the fact that Jasovic took the statement or if you think that there's any problem in this regard and if you intend to accept Mr. Nice's objections, I'm not opposed to having Mr. Jasovic appear here and being asked a question or two as the authorised official who took the statement. That would be the first time I see the man, of course, because I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That will be a matter for you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Robinson. If he's here, he can appear, as far as I'm concerned, so that I can ask him about that. It's just a detail. Perhaps it will take a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you wish that person to -- to appear, then you should inform the liaison officer and ask her to have the necessary arrangements made for him to testify, and we can organise for him to -- to be interposed so that he will not be inconvenienced severely. And you should do this by the break. Would you, Mr. Nice, then, be -- what would your position on that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know. I only heard some of the cross-examination yesterday which gives rise to matters about which I'm very interested but which might well require further consideration by us. In any event, the witness is due to be cross-examined this afternoon and I don't know whether that's going to extend into tomorrow, but I felt it probably my duty to make sure the accused knew what the position -- the rather unusual position was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I shall also be dealing with this witness when we come to look at the exhibit position at the end of this witness. So may I suggest we deal with things sequentially but the accused is now in possession of the knowledge I thought he ought to have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, take charge of the matter. Consult with the liaison officer and make your decision. Inform us as soon as possible, and no later than the first break, however. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Marinkovic, yesterday Mr. Nice questioned you about your husband's participation in the protests that had to do with the position of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He said literally that it was quite clear that you took part in activities aimed at supporting my policy against the non-Serbs. That was the definition used by Mr. Nice. Do you know about this? Throughout that time in Serbia, was there any policy against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, since you're a Macedonian, you're not a Serb yourself, tell me, you personally, since you're a Macedonian and since you have lived and continue to live until the present day in Serbia, have you ever had the least bit of a problem due to the fact that you're a Macedonian rather than a Serb?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I never had any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout this time of crisis and wars in the former Yugoslavia from 1991 all the way up to the Dayton agreement in 1995, are you aware of any persecution of Muslims, Croats, or some other national minority in Serbia in any way?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice said that the protesters from Kosovo went to Vojvodina to bring down the Vojvodina government, as he put it. Do you know why the protesters from Kosovo went to different towns throughout Yugoslavia during those years, that is to say the years we're talking about, that is; 1988, 1989? Or, rather, I think that most of these activities took place in 1988. Why did they go?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I lived in Pristina at the time, that is to say in Kosovo and Metohija, at that time the Serbs organised these protests so that the rest in Serbia, Vojvodina included, could see how poor their status was in Kosovo and Metohija, that they could not live because of the violence that was launched at that time by the Albanian separatists against the Serbs and other non-Albanians in Kosovo. At that time they were second-rate citizens. They had no rights. They could not take part in government. They could not get employment. They could not present their status and the fact that they were oppressed there. At that time, all of us who lived there had the feeling that we were living in Albania rather than in Serbia. Very little was known about that in other towns. That is why the Serbs raised their voice, because they could not take the separatists' terror any longer. Pressure was brought to bear against the Serbs in different ways, and a great many Serbs moved out at the time. They left Kosovo and Metohija in order to protect their families, especially their children. I can say as a parent, as a mother - at that time I had two children - that I and the other Serbs who lived in Kosovo and Metohija had to take our own children to school and to meet them in front of school after their lessons because Albanian children would attack our children and bully them. Albanian separatists were bringing pressure to bear and exercising violence against us, and that is why the Serbs wanted to tell the mother country Serbia what was going on so that the state, Serbia, could take measures to protect them against Albanian separatists. I'm telling you this as a citizen who lived in Kosovo and Metohija and who felt that throughout my stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Marinkovic. Apart from these reasons, that is to say seeking to have their own rights exercised and drawing the attention of the Yugoslav public to their bad position, were there any other reasons why Serbs went to towns throughout Yugoslavia and held these rallies?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no other reason. Everybody knows, whoever is listening to this now, Albanians and Serbs, that I'm telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Marinkovic. We're not going to dwell on this subject much longer because we have to save time. Now I would like to put some questions to you in relation to what Mr. Nice asserted; namely, that there were tortures in prison. So briefly, the subject would be torture in prisons in order to obtain statements under duress from some prisoners. Was there any torture in prisons?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no torture in prisons because that is prohibited by law, and it is not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking about what the law says and whether the law bans that. There is no doubt about that. I'm asking you the following: In spite of the fact that this is prohibited by law, was there any torture in prisons that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice said here that it was the police that tortured prisoners. Please explain this to us: When a prisoner is in prison or if a person is remanded in custody as a detainee, does the said person have any contact with the police?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A suspect, after having been heard by the investigating judge and after having been detained if there are legal grounds for detention, the police has no further contact or any jurisdiction with regard to the said person. The said person then falls under the jurisdiction of the district prison, which has its own rules and its own Code of Conduct. As regards everything that has to do with the status of detainees, that falls under the prison officials where the said detainee is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the employees in the prison, the prison guards and other persons employed there at the correction facilities? Are they employed by the police or the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are employees of the Ministry of Justice because district courts fall under the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the staff working in prison, including guards in uniform, are not members of the police force. They are, rather, employees of the Ministry of Justice; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going back to my original question: Can they have any contact with the police in prison?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of any incident when a prison guard interrogated a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, in your documentation, in your capacity as an investigating judge, you dealt with statements given by detainees; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, since you explained that, when statements are taken from detainees, in addition to yourself, the Prosecutor is present, the Defence attorney for the suspect, an interpreter, and I assume a clerk taking notes. Was this the usual practice in every case when such statements were taken?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Maybe I've misunderstood, but the statements were put to you yesterday. Were they all taken in your presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it has been put to you that you're always present when statements are taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the statements that were put to me yesterday were not statements made by suspects or accused persons. These were citizens who were giving statements at the SUP, whereas I take statements from suspects and accused persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, tell me now, these statements made before you in your capacity as investigating judge and in the presence of the Defence attorney, the Prosecutor, and the other officials involved, are they correctly taken in all your records of investigation? Are these statements only the ones that you took in the presence of all these persons, or was anything ever added to these statements? For example, it was said here that some statement was given under duress. So since this could not have taken place in the presence of all these five people, could anything be added to what was said to you in the presence of all these five officials?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered in the record, in the notes, only what the person who was making the statement said. When the person would present his defence, I would dictate that to the note-taking clerk, and that is exactly what the note-taking clerk would type out. Then the record would be read back to the suspect, and I'd always ask whether the said person agrees with everything that became part of the record, and that is what it means when it says that the said person takes the statement and accepts it as his own, and the person has to sign every page of the statement. Also, the interpreter who was present has to sign every page, I have to as well, and also the recording clerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice gave a few statements here or, rather, records of examinations of detainees. In all cases except for one, what was established was light bodily injuries. I don't have to actually count them now. Five, six reports by the commission, the medical commission. In one case, the medical commission established that no injuries were found. So we're going to leave that particular record aside. So in a few cases, light bodily injuries were found. As an experienced investigating judge, can you say what can be the cause of light bodily injury in the case of detainees, injuries established by a medical commission?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what? That could mean that the person fell in the prison premises, and it's -- it's a mere fall that can cause such injury. I'm saying this from my practice, from my experience. In relation to that, I gave instructions for the doctors to describe the injuries involved and to say how grave they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, when you would get a request or if you would be warned that a detainee had been injured, did you ever not give orders to a doctor to examine him?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember - it's been a long time now - I always acted on these written requests, and I always sent instructions to the prison administration for the said person to be examined by a doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Excuse me. Judge Marinkovic, I couldn't follow that part of your evidence. How were you able to conclude that -- you don't like the word "conclude." How could you find out that those prisoners just fell in the premises of the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would just assume that that's how light bodily injury occurred in view of my years of experience in these cases. That is usually how light bodily injury could take place. It's just an assumption, but I cannot establish it for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. May I continue, Mr. Kwon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any cases of the prisoners coming to blows amongst themselves in prison?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, things like that did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what could have been the reasons for light bodily injury, for example?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what you just asked. They might have had a fight amongst themselves and then hit each other with their fists, and then this would result in that kind of injury during a brawl.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The ones we heard about yesterday were all, according to the doctors' reports, inflicted by a heavy blow from a blunt heavy mechanical implement. We were talking yesterday about clearly described injuries. They're called minor, I assume, because there were no broken bones involved, and there was no suggestion that these were caused by fights or accidents or anything of that nature. So why don't we deal with actuality and deal with the questions that were actually asked yesterday rather than speculation and -- about matters that were never addressed in the cross-examination at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Your Honour will also remember that yesterday I raised with the witness the question of whether she had a particular matter in mind, whether she had delayed examination until the injuries faded was the other way the matter was put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please answer the question put by Mr. Nice. He asked you yesterday - I don't remember your answer - but did you delay the investigation or examination until the injuries had faded or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not true. That's not correct. It's just the administration that takes awhile, all the paperwork through the court, the prison, to make an appointment for a medical examination at the institute when they have a free space. Otherwise, there was no reason for it to be deployed or prolonged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much time would elapse usually, Mrs. Marinkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't tell you exactly but roughly -- well, it depended from one case to the next, depending on the workload. Because when you send in a request to the prison authorities it is up to them to organise it, because from a prison to hospital it's quite a distance. I don't know how many kilometres. So you have to organise the transport, you have to find the guards to escort the detainee and take him to hospital, and then you have to make an appointment at the hospital itself in advance to have a free slot. And once you have made an appointment, then the detainee is taken there. It might be a week, ten days, 15 days, depending on the organisation and the facilities in those two institutions. It doesn't depend on me. But as I say, there were no urgent cases which required emergency measures where life or limb was at risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, one point again. The Court has yet to decide about the admissibility of the medical certificates, but it has both the requests which are dated and the report of the examination, which are dated, and the Court may notice a coincidence with dates; namely, the requests and the examinations are actually on the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just thank Mr. Nice. If this was done on the same day, then when the Defence counsel tabled a request, the examination was carried out straight away so there can be no question of delay or postponement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see the dates yesterday. I didn't pay attention to that. I don't know whether there was the date or whether I was told in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mrs. Marinkovic. Now, tell me, as an experienced investigating judge yourself, as all these cases were classified as light bodily injuries, for anybody suffering light bodily injuries can we say that they were beaten up at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't see how the witness can answer that properly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I assumed that in practice, in the practice of an investigating judge, they would be able to assess whether somebody had been beaten or not on the basis of what we've been saying here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic has constantly told us it is not her job to draw that sort of conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move on to the next question, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Milosevic. I have further points to clarify once again. Could you wait, give me a minute. Mr. Nice, you said that the request of the -- the request and the report of the examination are dated on the same day?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the medical report was done in December 1994, and the further complaint -- ah, yes. Complaint was made at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Complaints made later. The chronology is, as the Prosecution would advance it, to take the particular example, but any of them, number one, Aliu Isak, a complaint by a lawyer made a month before, application for examination made on the 22nd of December, examination conducted on the 22nd of December, complaint by lawyer to judge of non-compliance with his request and complaints comes later in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The point I'd like to clarify is that whether there is a further examination according to the -- this complaint, is this witness's position that she's not in the position to answer that question because she has not the records in its entirety or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That I'm not sure. I think she'll have to answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, can you answer that question, whether there is a further examination according to the complaint filed to you and various institutions saying that his client was beaten up again in February 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was like this: I can't really say now because I don't have the complete files with me. If I had the case files in front of me, I'd be able to see, because it's all there, all the papers, all the documents. For each of my actions note was taken and there is a written trace of what was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Marinkovic, yesterday Mr. Nice asked you something about an investigation you conducted about the formation of an illegal MUP in Kosovo and Metohija. Do you remember that? Do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you conduct the investigation with respect to the organisation of this illegal MUP or the illegal police of the Albanian separatists in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, are you waiting for the interpretation to appear on the transcript? I can see that we have a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I'm bearing in mind the interpreters. They have asked me to speak more slowly so I'm looking at the monitor and once the translation finishes there, then I give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ah, I see. I thought that was it. That's the transcript. The interpretation is quicker, so you don't have to make that long a pause, to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. save time. The case was against how many suspects?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eighty-nine individuals in the pre-trial investigation phase, and that was the requirement made by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the indictment was raised against how many individuals?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The indictment was against 72 persons. May I just take a look and make sure? Yes. The indictment was against 72 individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many of those were found guilty at the end of the trial and the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sixty-nine were found guilty, having committed crimes specified in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in those activities, the activities they were charged with and found guilty of, and they not only represent the criminal act of association, as was suggested, but it was also procurement of weapons, included procurement of weapons and certain other actions that were dangerous to individuals and society as a whole.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the investigation, on the basis of the statements of persons interviewed and on the basis of the proof and evidence that I amassed during the investigative phase, we were able to see that not only did they work to prepare this illegal MUP, but they also worked on the procurement of weapons illegally, and in order to do so they visited areas in the area of Macedonia, towards Macedonia, because they were not able to procure weapons and import weapons from Albania illegally.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: They were. Interpreter's correction: They were able to import weapons illegally from Albania. Could the accused repeat his question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything they did to prepare and form the illegal MUP, they represented this and wanted it to appear as if it was a sort of trade union work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what Mrs. Kandic says in some of her articles. And what was established during the investigation? Was it trade union activity or was it some other form of activity?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the investigation that I conducted, we established that they had in fact been working illegally to set up hostile -- a hostile association. Prior to previous instructions from the government in exile and at the initiative of that government, they were working to form and establish centres of public and state securities in seven towns all over Kosovo and Metohija. They had established their network of associates which worked to collect information about monitoring the police and army of Yugoslavia and monitoring individual inspectors as well and their work. They also monitored Albanians whom they considered to be collaborators of the police and collected information, and that information was coded and sent to the government of Kosovo, Kosovo Republic. The information was collected and amassed by being introduced into computers under codes. They were encrypted and then they would send them on both to the government and the President Rugova, their President Rugova, and also to their Assembly. These were all illegal organs parallelly formed and parallel to state institutions that existed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, you said that Albanians were monitored as well and surveillance organised of Albanians as well whom they suspected as being collaborators and collaborating with state organs. Now, these individuals whom you say they treated as being collaborators of Serbia and Yugoslavia and who were under surveillance by this illegal MUP, were they -- did they run any danger? Were they open to danger?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. By working on the investigation, the information that was gathered with respect to surveillance of these individuals, by force of chance once again I myself as an investigating judge went on site to look into a case of two Albanians whom they considered to be collaborators of the Serb police force, and they were killed. Those two persons were killed. One was a porter who worked in the municipality building or the municipality building in Glogovac and a postman working in the post office in Glogovac. Those were the two people in question. One man's name was Ymer Lako, and the postman was Mustafa Kurtaj. With respect to those two individuals, I went to conduct an on-site investigation and there is a record of that. Ymer Lako was killed in 1998 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... once again, and I have to observe that although the Court will remember we were faced with whatever it was, just under 40 files, I explained I'd look at parts of one of them, and I looked at it for the purposes essentially dealing with the treatment of the prisoners by -- or the accused -- hands of this witness. I went into the detail hardly at all. If the Court wants to hear the details from this witness, so be it. I will have to deal with the material, or I may choose to deal with the material with another witness but I certainly haven't gone into the substance of the police trial in any detail at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with both points made by Mr. Nice, Mr. Milosevic. Mrs. Marinkovic, if you're going to read from a document, then that should be brought to the attention of the Court so we can know what it is and make our own determination as to whether it's appropriate for you to read from it. Mr. Milosevic, I think you are going a little wide of the mark here, and you are in fact raising matters that did not arise in cross-examination. As Mr. Nice said, he cross-examined this witness as to her role in the treatment of prisoners that were subjected to her care, and I believe this is -- this is wide of the mark. So move on to another topic. In any event, I think you are spending too long on the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, what are you reading from? Tell us first of all.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading from tab 1 that has been distributed to everyone. That is my short overview of the cases in which I was investigative judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Just let us know before. If you're going to read from a document, let us know what you're reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we have the translation of this this morning, so I'm afraid it hasn't been possible for me to review it in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we don't have the translation at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tab 1.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I wish to draw your attention to one thing. The questions I'm putting now to Judge Marinkovic do not relate to the treatment of prisoners. That issue was dealt with before. These questions deal with the claim of Mr. Nice that the regime prosecuted trade unions, in support of which he provided the text by Natasa Kandic. This illegal MUP was represented as the trade union of Albanians, of Albanian policemen, and the result of that was the death and killing of some Albanians. The information gathered concerned persons who allegedly collaborated with Serbia, and these people were later killed. So this was obviously not a trade organisation, as Mr. Nice tried to present it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you have dealt with it sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell me now, Mrs. Marinkovic, so this was an illegal Ministry of the Interior, established by Kosovo separatists. Did you know that a parallel schooling system, a parallel health care system were established, and other parallel institutions, including political ones? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The organisation of parallel schooling, health care, and any other - how shall I put it? - non-aggressive activities, were they ever prosecuted by the police or the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not allowing any more questions along those lines. Move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, among the things Mr. Nice presented yesterday, there was a document that is the letter to the Serbian public sent by a great number of people including nine bulleted points expressing certain demands. It starts with, "Dear Sirs."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to draw your attention, gentlemen, to this translation into English which is provided along with the Serbian text. It is not actually a translation of that text.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I made clear yesterday -- I made it clear that it was not a translation of the text in the newspaper article in which the petition was, I think, photographed, but was a text from another newspaper and it contained just the relevant nine points. I also made it plain at that stage that because the witness at that stage was really denying any knowledge of the petition, that I wasn't going to press ahead with questioning her about it. It happened that later, despite her earlier answers, she seemed to have rather full recall of it. And if the accused wishes to bring the petition in, so be it, but my intention was, in light of her not remembering the petition, to deal with it with a later witness. So the accused may be wasting time unless he wishes that the petition should now be dealt with by her, in which case I'm happy for the document to serve the purpose, and the only purpose I would rely on was the format of the petition and the nine points for which there is a translation in English but from a different newspaper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what exactly is the point you wish to raise? Mr. Nice didn't rely on the document, so it's difficult to see how anything could arise from it. You would have to persuade us that the question that you wish to raise arises in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you weren't seeking to have this document admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wasn't. I was going to mention today when we come to exhibits that, as far as I was concerned, at the time I'd withdrawn it. Although I was going to observe, as I already have, that the witness seemed to have acknowledged it's rather better later, but so what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to draw your attention to the fact that this exhibit as presented with the English and Serbian texts, the English and Serbian are actually quite different. May I continue, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't understand the point you just made. Is this a different document? I see. Okay. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English text is a translation of some article from the Borba newspaper, whereas the Serbian text is an open letter published in the Nin magazine. Those are two different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not going to deal with this anyway, because Mr. Nice is not tendering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, just a few things in relation to these statements we received yesterday, statements that were taken from a number of persons who had previously given statements to authorised officers at the time of the incident in Racak. I'm not certain that I will go in the same order as yesterday, but I would like to go through them briefly. Mr. Nice provided the statement of Emini Shemsi, which is understand 47, and this Emini Shemsi said that he had been beaten by baseball bats. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the recording, the video that I saw yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what he said. Several video clips were seen yesterday, and this person said on the screen that he had been beaten by baseball bats.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, in Kosovo and Metohija, have you ever heard of anyone playing baseball and have you ever seen a baseball bat in the entire Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no idea about this game, and I have never seen that bat. I don't know what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Americans will be disappointed to hear that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am not interested in sports. As a woman, I have a lot of other things to do. And I have never had occasion to travel to the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, another statement we have here is that of Muhadin Dzeljadini, who says that he did not wish to sign his previous statement, but after seeing blood in the basement, he got frightened and signed anyway. Do you remember who took this statement from Dzeljadini? I mean, which SUP took the statement?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the statement in front of me, but it was taken by the authorised officers of SUP Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever been to SUP Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you have, were you able to determine whether there are any rooms inside that SUP where detained persons were beaten?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The place where I visited, where I waited for the investigative team to arrive and to accompany me on a on-site investigation, I was not able to see anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice said that it was well known that under the regime of that time some prisoners were tortured. Do you know whether after the 5th of October, when I was no longer president, anyone was released from prison apart from Albanian terrorists? Was there anyone to release?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, only Albanians were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were Mazreku brothers among those released, the people who -- the bothers who incinerated those people in Klecka?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, Mr. Nice said that through a combination of circumstance - and I believe this relates to tab 52, I can't remember exactly at this moment -- which was that tab that one of the authorised officers taking the statement was Jasovic, was that 52?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We were informed that he was here yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My understanding was that he was the interviewing officer in all of them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So much the better. I can't remember which is which. I'll look at the tabs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it was always two persons together who took the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this particular one testified in Limaj case yesterday and we will call him too. Now, tell me this: In this statement, he said that he had not signed the previous statement, that it was not his statement therefore.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I would require a handwriting analysis, because we have handwriting on both statements that can be compared in the statement of Mustafa Afrim, although it must be said that in this last statement given last week he tried to bend it to the left a little to make it look a little different, but I would demand a handwriting analysis to be performed so that we can establish the truth, whether this is really his handwriting on the statement of the 16th of January, 1999, or not. It is pretty obvious to me that it is the same signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you wish to call a handwriting expert, Mr. Milosevic, that's a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then I will set it aside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you indicated yesterday that it was likely that that would be done anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a course that's obviously open to us to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be helpful if a person could be identified to do it. The accused could be consulted about that person and just one analysis was done and we were all agreed to proceed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we reach that position, but I'm going to ask for discussion about exhibits generally in any event first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're not experts in handwriting, but we can look at the handwriting ourselves. That happens frequently in some jurisdictions. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you this, Mrs. Marinkovic, because he claims now that somebody signed the statement for him. Look what he says in the statement. "Since I live in Racak village --" Do you have this statement in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask the usher to provide this statement to the witness. It's tab 52.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let tab 52 be provided to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you referring to tab 52 or the statement taken by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both, actually. The Prosecution, though, has only statements in English. I have this statement in English as well, but it makes no sense to give it to Mrs. Marinkovic because she doesn't understand English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mrs. Marinkovic, please look at this. I will only quote from point 3 of this statement, which was taken by one of Mr. Nice's investigators or employees on the 3rd of April. In point 3 it says that he started to scream and yell at him, saying that he was a member of the KLA. In this statement which he signed and now is trying to disown that signature, does it say anywhere in that statement that he was a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. And I noticed that straight away yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now please look at this statement, because it is rather specific. It is not broad or general, nor does it refer to general issues. He says: "Since I live in Racak village, I know and I saw with my own eyes that the substaff of the KLA in Racak village is located in the house of Mustafa Suceri Sefa. The commander is Afet Bilalli, Musliu Shefqet is his deputy." It's the very beginning of the statement. There are no paragraphs here, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what is the question that you wish to put?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the question is: Since quite a number of specific facts are cited here, can we surmise that the authorised officers who took the statement from him just dreamt up these things and made him sign?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's not a proper question at all, and you well know it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, the facts collected in relation to the situation in Racak in general, do they coincide with these assertions as to who the commander of the substaff was, who these different persons were, I mean all the information obtained through them?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The facts that this citizen Mustafa Afrim presented in his statement do coincide with the other statements that were taken in relation to what happened in Racak, and we found quite a bit of material evidence on the ground as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If we look at the tabs pertaining to the statements of these witnesses who now say that they gave them out of fear and one person says that he didn't even sign the statement because it's not his signature, is it obvious that these statements largely overlap and in terms of other matters they do not overlap depending on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. That's -- that's a comment, it's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mrs. Marinkovic, in the second paragraph of his statement, it says that "Members of the KLA in the village of Racak have checkpoints in the following places: In front of the bridge in Racak, next to the asphalt road on the right-hand side of the former shop of Mustafa Metus, at a place called Cesta, on the hill above the old people's home..." and so on and so forth. Is that what was indeed established there?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Many citizens who were interviewed confirmed this fact, and we actually saw it on the ground because the old people's home had been targeted by the terrorists, and there were visible traces from projectiles on that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In his statement, he says that he was told that he was a member of the KLA. In this statement of his in 1999 it does not say that he was a member of the KLA. He mentions that they forced him to touch some wires. Mrs. Marinkovic, since you're an investigating judge, if we're talking about electric shock -- how should I put this? When a burn is sustained during electric shocks, I mean, do these burns remain or, rather, the scars, do they remain permanent?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness has no experience of torture or people being tortured so I'm not sure how she can possibly answer a question about the effect of electric shocks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Mr. Milosevic, that's time wasting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not electric shocks, but as an ordinary citizen, I can say on the basis of my own experience, too, if you burn your skin, I mean, there's always a scar, and I've experienced that myself in everyday life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you might as well ask me the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mrs. Marinkovic. Do you know whether any police authorities used any devices for torturing prisoners? Specifically I'm asking you about electric shocks, to use the expression used by Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any complaints from any defence attorneys of any accused person that some kind of electric shocks were applied in the case of his client?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document that was compiled in Urosevac. This is more than two months prior to the outbreak of the war. This person says, at the end of the third paragraph in his statement, that one of the persons who was working on a computer and finally one of them said, "Let him go, he's a child." So, Mrs. Marinkovic, they said let him go, he's a child. Since we're talking about a town where there's normal life, I mean it's not some remote backwater, had he truly been exposed to some kind of electric shocks, could he have addressed the judiciary organs, the government, the president of the municipality, anybody?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you continue in this vein, we are going to terminate the re-examination. The witness can't help you very much on this statement. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you wish to refute it, there are other means open to you to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not refuting it. It's Mr. Nice who is refuting it, in his own assertions and through his exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice asked you yesterday, Mrs. Marinkovic, in relation to Racak whether you interviewed the inhabitants of the village of Racak when you came there. Do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the village of Racak when you came there, when you finally managed on the 18th, as you explained to us, to get in. You made several attempts. First you tried to get in on the 15th and then the next day they wouldn't let you get near when Walker was there and then you had to withdraw again and then ultimately you managed to get in on 18th. Were there any citizens there who you could have put questions to?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The village was abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in addition to -- except for those 40 corpses you found in the mosque, there was not a living soul in the village; is that your assertion?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You then toured the environs of Racak.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you wrote about trenches, casings, bunkers, and so on and so forth. Were there any other corpses except for those that you found in the mosque?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The representatives of the OSCE were with you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody mention that there were some other bodies there too?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In relation to this, I can say that after that, when the corpses were supposed to be handed over to the families, I had several conversations and contacts with the local villagers and the representatives of the mosques both in Racak and in Stimlje, with the representatives of the verification mission who were in charge of Stimlje and Urosevac. We met and we discussed the hand-over of the bodies. On all those days, whenever I went to Stimlje, none of the citizens who were in contact with me mentioned anything new, saying that they were eyewitnesses or that they had anything to add. They had the opportunity of doing so because we talked to them at length, and then after that the members of the families came to Pristina to get the bodies. So they had ample opportunity. If they had something new to offer, they had several occasions to talk to me and also to address higher instances than myself; the OSCE, the representatives of the mosques, and people from Stimlje. I have notes about all these contacts I had with them for days and all the names of the persons I contacted are listed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just to go back to the question Mr. Milosevic asked you as to whether there were any persons in the village when you went there on the 19th to whom you could put questions, you said there were no persons there to whom you could put questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On the 18th. But as I understand your testimony, even if there were persons, your testimony is that, according to your procedures, you would not have been able, you would not have had the capacity to put questions to those persons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I could only record their names and then give them to the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, during your examination-in-chief, you indicated that the names did not match the persons who were killed in Racak, that is, and the persons whose names are listed on Mr. Nice's lists. Mr. Nice asked you about this yesterday and his suggestion was that Albanians often change their names. Can this fact that the names do not match be due to changes of names among Albanians or is it simply a mismatch?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The names on the list in the indictment and on my list do not match.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm going to ask you something very briefly in relation to Mr. Nice's questions that had to do with the prison in Dubrava. So you had official contacts with what was in your territory. Isn't that right, Mrs. Marinkovic?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When persons from the Dubrava prison were transferred to your territory through the municipality of Lipljan, which is under the district court in Pristina, you then went to carry out an on-site investigation. We showed all of that through the exhibits. Do you know how many prisoners and detainees were transferred from Dubrava prison to Lipljan or to some other prisons?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figure, but I know that a great many were transferred, those who were injured and those were not injured. That is to say that all the detainees from Istok were transferred to Lipljan, because Dubrava, the prison of Dubrava was completely destroyed and it was not possible to stay there any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you say "a great many," what do you mean by "a great many"? What is the order of magnitude? I can understand that you cannot give us the exact figure now, but what is the order of magnitude? What is a great many: 100, 200, 500? How many prisoners, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you an exact figure now, but it must be around a hundred. Now, I cannot say whether it's a bit more or a bit less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I hope we will be able to establish that. On page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, how many did you interview among them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not interview them because on the day when I was there, people were still in shock and stressed out. They were given medical assistance. But we agreed with the prison administration that once these persons recover, a few days later those who were not in prison but those who remained in the Lipljan prison would be interviewed in order to be able to find out what it was that happened in Dubrava. So later on, after that, I received information that a number of detainees were interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to see the statements of these persons? Mr. Kwon asked you about this just now. You did not interview them, but did you have the statements of these detainees as to what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I restricted my questions for want of time to the mere confirmation that she was dependent on the material of her colleague and I left it there. My recollection is, and we can look at the transcript, there have been several questions asked indeed by the Bench about the circumstances in which the colleague had produced his material, problems about the dates and one thing and another. It seemed to me that that was the appropriate way to leave it, given that I have to make a selection of the topics I'm going to cover. I confirmed with her that she hadn't spoken to the three eyewitnesses that were relied on by -- surviving eyewitnesses relied on by the Prosecution, and I left it at that. It doesn't seem to me very much scope for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. She confirmed that she's not well aware of the happenings in 22nd and 23rd -- oh, no, 23rd and 24th. Proceed. Ask another question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson [as interpreted]. But she explained that she did not interview these persons, but she did say yesterday during her cross-examination that statements had been taken from these prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So do you know anything about these statements, Mrs. Marinkovic?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to these statements, I know about them because during the break I had, I checked the court files regarding these statements. Whether they were in the court and whether we had them. I found the statements, I photocopied them, but since I'm not in contact with the Defence, with Mr. Milosevic's advisors, I have those statements and I can offer them to the Trial Chamber in order to clarify the situation and everything that happened in Dubrava. Because the prisoners who were in Istok and who had been wounded and injured wrote these statements in their own hand and explained what happened in the prison of Dubrava; from the beginning of the bombing, how the bombing took place, how NATO planes targeted the area, what it was that was targeted. So if the Trial Chamber believes that it could be of assistance in order to clarify the situation in Dubrava, I can now offer you these documents into evidence if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you said that the Prosecutor who was in charge of this investigation is in 65 ter witness list of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I said that. I think we checked that last time. Yes, he is. And I'm just trying to look at yesterday's transcript. If the witness says that she spoke of statements being taken, then I'm not going to challenge that, but I'd like just to check it. But even if she did volunteer it in answer to the very limited questioning that I put of her, that doesn't let those statements in. I haven't seen these statements that she's going to rely upon. They might raise exactly the same sorts of issues or different issues from the kind I've had to raise with the three statements that we were able to deal with over the break. So on two grounds -- or three grounds, I would invite the Chamber not to consider allowing in this material at this stage. And if it does, I might have to ask for leave at some later stage to cross-examine this witness on them if there's no other witness I can deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you would be entitled to. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just calling up the record myself on the LiveNote and I've just found the passage where Mr. Nice, questioning the witness, said: "... to deal with a couple of other things. So far as Dubrava Prison is concerned, you interviewed no survivors other than the ones you say who were injured and moved into the location ... You interviewed no other survivors, did you? No, yes, right. Just let me say, and you didn't wait for me to complete my answer, since a large number of people were injured, I did have the opportunity of -- and that people had been moved, I did have an opportunity of seeing them, however, I wasn't able to talk to them directly because they were under stress..." The witness gave further details. "We agreed with the prison authorities to talk to the people in question so that they --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is invited to quote question and answer when quoting from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "We agreed with the prison authorities to talk to them, to the people in question, so that they could tell them what had happened while they were in Dubrava in the prison there." And then: "You produced your colleagues' report which we've looked at on the last occasion we were here ..." And it's referred to the fact that he didn't speak to any of the survivors who had given evidence in this court. "I don't know who these people were," the answer is. So it's clear that there were statements that were taken as part of an investigation, and that is what this particular witness is offering the Court at this stage, which arose from Mr. Nice's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It could be produced later, through the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They could be marked for identification now, as we had done in the Prosecution case, if you remember, when documents were produced; marked for identification, and then dealt with by the more appropriate witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I think that's the appropriate course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be heard on that? Actually, the answer that -- I've found it now myself. She was asked specifically if she interviewed no other survivors, and her answer was no. And then she volunteered as much as to say we agree that the prison authorities -- with the prison authorities to talk to the people in question. As a matter of fact, she doesn't go on to say what the process was and the topic changed from there. If she had said something about "and took statements," then I might at that stage have asked for them. I really must press that the time has come to draw a line in this extensive re-examination and to say that this is yet another example of the accused trying to get material in in re-examination that I simply wasn't on notice to deal with and haven't dealt with and, what's more, didn't deal with because I took the specific decision. In order to be economic in the use of time, that this was a topic that I would not trouble with because of the way it had been dealt with in chief, which I simply underline, so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the -- if they're marked for identification, no questions are asked except to confirm that these are the statements obtained the way the witness got them. You then have the advantage that you've got them rather than hoping they'll turn up before the witness who comes to speak to them turns up, and you have the additional advantage that they won't get in unless the witness comes and speaks to the way in which they were prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's true. I accept the practical good sense of that as a proposition which accords in practical effect with what I'm asking then, that the matter not be covered in re-examination, so I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will mark them for identification, and Mr. Milosevic, then you will seek to produce them through the appropriate witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, for the record, Mr. Nice has explained that he didn't know about the statements and then couldn't take them into consideration. I assume that from the statement by the witness that you could have heard that I didn't know about the statements either because the witness found them subsequently. So I don't know what it actually says in those statements. I wanted to ask her to read out the names and to read out what it says in the statements. But if you consider that this should be introduced in some other way, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. That's our decision, and we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Robinson, the witness that was mentioned by Mr. Nice a moment ago with respect to tab 52, will he be able to appear now or not? Because I don't want to detain this witness any more. I have no more questions for witness Mrs. Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, whether that person comes as a witness doesn't affect Mrs. Marinkovic. If you are finished your re-examination, and you should be, then she can go. Let me finish. And it's not very clear to me that that person would be able to come immediately after Mrs. Marinkovic. You would need to -- to speak to that person, no doubt, if you're going to call that person as a witness. You would have to work through the liaison officer and make the necessary arrangements. So as I said before, we'll give you the 20-minute break to have that discussion, and if you wish to call that person as a witness, then the person will be called at the -- at the earliest opportunity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I had one more question just briefly, not to keep the witness until after the break. May I ask it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, in Schedule 1, page 57 of the indictment, we have the names of persons, as it says, killed in the prison in Dubrava, whose names are well known, and then we have 26 individuals listed there. Do you know how many people lost their lives during the bombing of the Dubrava Prison?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This doesn't arise. I asked no questions on this topic and if it wasn't dealt with by me he cannot ask questions about it in re-examination. Had this topic been covered in chief, I might have taken a different course in cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Marinkovic, that concludes your testimony. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you may leave when we are adjourned. We are going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, on the question of the admissibility of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Before I turn to the exhibits that I would seek to produce, can I invite the Chamber to consider the position of all those exhibits bearing the name of Dragan Jasovic - I'll give you the numbers of them in a second - and invite you to decide that they should no longer be or should not be exhibits in this case. They are -- I've forgotten the number of the overall exhibit, but within this last witness's exhibit they are tabs 46 -- it's D290. Tabs 46, tab 47, tab 48, tab 51, tab 52, and tab 54. My application is based on the grounds that -- as follows: For hearsay to be admitted - we've travelled -- travelled this road before but I must set it out - the material has to be reliable, has to be indicia of reliability. The Chamber will also have in mind, although it's not determinative of this issue, but will have in mind that Rule 95 also specifies the exclusion of evidence obtained by methods which cast doubt upon its reliability or if the admission is antithetical to or would damage the integrity of the proceedings. A very brief reminder of the recent history of similar exhibits would be to the following effect: That with Andric, interviews were produced and are exhibits, counter-material in the form of video recordings of one of the people interviewed explaining and thus denying the content of the interview rejected. In Lituchy, interviews admitted but a statement taken by one of the people interviewed admitted as a Prosecution exhibit. And we then turn to this last witness. Looking at those two previous examples, in Andric the person whose words the accused seeks to rely on, that is the person interviewed, was interviewed by a journalist, not by the witness. In Lituchy, the person whose words the accused seeks to rely on, i.e., the person interviewed, was interviewed by Lituchy. In this last witness's case, the person whose words the accused wishes to rely on was interviewed not by the witness, not at all in the witness's presence, but by someone else who simply handed the document to the witness in some way. Again, Andric and Lituchy to some degree tangential. This material not tangential at all. If it be the case that a significant number of the people in gully were ever shown to be members of the KLA, then not only would there be consequences -- possible consequences for a count in this indictment but, bearing in mind the significance of the Racak event and the history overall, there might be rather broader implications. So this is important material potentially. I should, incidentally, say because it's something that I must ensure the accused knows, it's a definite parenthesis before I forgot it: The Chamber will recall that some of the evidence upon which we really to prove that people in Racak who were killed were not members of the KLA was someone called Shukri Buja. He -- and it's another of these interesting crossover realities of prosecuting all sides of a conflict. He has been a witness in the Limaj case on matters other than Racak. He was called by the Prosecution, but he was actually turned hostile by the Prosecution, and that's something that we're going to set out in a Rule 68 notification so that the accused, if he has missed it already, doesn't miss it. But you should know that before we move on. I come back to my theme: The Prosecution's position with all these categories of statements is that they should be excluded. Alternatively, if they are admitted, that then the counter-material should go in in order, as it were, for the time being to neutralise it, to neutralise its value for the truth of its content. But our base position, and I should also observe that these matters are under applications of two different kinds before Your Honours at the moment, but our basic position is that when material of this kind is produced, especially this last witness, for the truth of its content, the appropriate course would be for the person on whom the accused wishes to rely and who in all cases are available to be called and dealing with the particular witnesses subject to the tabs of Exhibit 290 to which I have referred, the Court will know that my learned friend Mr. Saxon and Investigator Jonathan Sutch went down over the course of what would have been a holiday. They found, without too much difficulty, three. One was recorded as dead, and the others they couldn't find in the time available. I should tell you also this: That they took careful steps to ensure that there was no inter-witness contamination, and indeed, as I'm informed, that when the witnesses were approached and spoken to and the topic of interest revealed to them, at a very early stage, with little or no prompting, they explained the circumstances that are subsequently set out both in the videotaped interviews of which we've seen very short extracts and in the summarised but signed statements that are before you. In short, looking at the Defence exhibits, our position is this: If you have two statements from the same person saying A and not A, saying one thing and then the reverse, then it would be quite impossible, in the absence of more, to choose between them and to say that one was reliable. This would apply as much to us, now that we know of the existence of the statements upon which the Defence relies if we wish to rely on our statements in written form, as it does to him. So that our position, Your Honours, to consider is that these statements as the accused would wish to produce them on an important matter simply do not have, in the light of the material we've now been able to provide to you before the close of the witness's evidence, they do not qualify as reliable and should not be admitted. The consequence of admitting them, it is said, is little different from the consequence of admitting hearsay in the Prosecution case, a proposition with which I respectfully differ -- from which I respectfully differ. First, the various examples of hearsay relied on in the Prosecution case were subject both to our shouldering the responsibility of establishing reliability, which we did in all cases, and where admitted was subject either to express arguments by my learned friend Mr. Kay, then amicus, arguments by the accused, and sometimes by simply, on each of their parts, concession that the exhibits should be produced. And this matter is dealt with in an annex, to some degree, to one of the recent filings by the Prosecution with which the Chamber may be acquainted. So that in fact in the Prosecution case the test for reliability was turned to and satisfied before the material was admitted. Here, the accused has not, in our respectful submission, done anything to satisfy you to the sufficient extent of the reliability of this material upon which he would seek to rely, and we would be left with these witness statements and any others adduced in the same way of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. importance with the following, I would invite you to say, unusual if not bizarre consequence: If the accused if able to call a witness such as the last witness who can produce a statement handed to her by a second party, I am barely able to ask any questions of the witness. Indeed, I was almost stopped from asking any questions of Ms. Marinkovic yesterday about the statements and the counter-statements, if I can so describe them, that I produced. If the statements then go into evidence, the following two odd consequences follow: One, if the matter is crucial or critical or even very important, I am obliged to make efforts to call the people, and yes, I could call these three people who have made statements over the last weekend, so that the person who seeks to rely on what they say doesn't call them and I do so that he can just cross-examine them, but more than that, the accused thereby gains an automatic extension of time for his case.
