Indeed, one could argue, by extension, that his best course if these statements are ruled admissible, would be to get the balance of his evidence wherever possible produced in statement forms, either handed to the witness or handed via an intermediary to the witness, in goes the evidence, and I'm told, well, if you don't like it, you've got to call the witness and then he's got to be to be available for cross-examination by the accused. It has, in our respectful submission, reached that potentially concerning position and we would invite you very seriously to reconsider it, to reconsider the position about these exhibits. Now, Your Honours, on questions of reliability you have the three statements, each of which were taken, and I can, of course, only explain to you what has been explained to me by Mr. Saxon and Mr. Sutch as to the circumstances but I hope that you will accept that, but we also have other material going to show unreliability and I invite you to look, for these purposes, without deciding on its admissibility, at this document Spotlight 16. And as we turn to it can I take a minute of your time to make something clear which I hope is clear but which may not be clear. The Court, and I understand why, is inclined to accord to a judge or a policeman coming from the former Yugoslavia the level of respect, deference that such an office holder in another country must justifiably attract. I must make it plain the Prosecution's view -- not the Prosecution's view, but the Prosecution's submissions on this general topic, if relevant, and if it needs to be argued on evidence in due course, will be that the police and the judicial system was acting as an arm of politics and must ultimately be considered at least potentially in that light and accorded no special deference. And indeed, if there is something if not concerning at least interesting about the degree to which this Court, in its efforts to be fair, super fair to this accused, excludes on the basis of potential unreliability sometimes the material of its own investigators who come here to meet the highest standards of human rights conduct, rejects that material because they may be thought to be partisan simply by working for the Office of the Prosecutor or the ICTY, and would be prepared to accept this material from the man Jasovic against whom there is now signed material going to show that he did the things asserted against him. With that observation in mind, can we look at Spotlight Number 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move onto it, you could help me, I think, to understand part of what you're saying. There's a lot of Prosecution evidence about, for example, persecutions, forcible transfer, and so on, which comes from reports compiled by interviewing refugees, and the reliability question, I assumed, was whether this was a genuine document in the sense that people went out and compiled it in the way in which they said, and that gave it a certain quality that enabled it to be admitted. I didn't understand that the reliability issue was whether all the witnesses who gave their stories were reliable. I thought that was a matter for the Trial Chamber to assess when it came to evaluate all the evidence. And similarly here, when you have a judge carrying out an investigation and gathering the material that others have prepared, I assumed the reliability question was, was what actually happened in the investigation, not whether people were tortured in the course of the carrying out of the inquiry. That was something we would have to assess on a different basis. Now, your submission doesn't proceed in that way. You're mixing all aspects of reliability together and saying we've got to make a judgement about the quality of the evidence in our ultimate consideration before we decide whether to admit it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I certainly hope I'm not mixing questions of reliability. In dealing with Your Honour's question in the like two parts: Where material was produced at the Prosecution's hand, Human Rights Watch reports, OSCE, matters of that sort, there was extensive evidence given by the compilers of the circumstances in which and of the disinterested character in the part of the staff employed the materials obtained. Sorry, it's a long and unattractive sentence but you know what I mean. They give evidence that their staff were drawn from here, there, and everywhere and were properly trained and that they produced the material in a routine and satisfactory way. Now, it may be, to pick up Your Honour's potential distinction, that in allowing the evidence in at that stage, both issues of reliability were in everybody's minds, that then the method of production being directly shown to be reliable, that is to say this is -- these are the questionnaires, they were prepared by my staff, they were processed and I took overall responsibility for the compiling of the report, as one of the witnesses might have said. But also, that if you have hundreds of witnesses -- or not witnesses, hundreds of people answering questions and an overall conclusion in the form of composite reports of the kind we've seen being prepared, then there is sufficient indicia over all of reliability of the content for it to be relied upon as to the truth or the general truth of its content.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, and probably to slow down, but ... I apologise if I get carried away a little bit. So my recollection -- I suppose we'd have to look at the arguments more fully to check whether the distinction that Your Honour draws was in our minds, but with that distinction in mind, I think that the documents were dealt with for reliability on both bases at the time. Now, reliability here is on the following basis: I have assumed reliability so that, in the absence of more evidence, the Court can rely on this or may rely on this for the truth of its content. Let me say at once if the Court says that even though these documents are produced there is no question of the Court relying on the content at all without more, either coming from the named witness and the named people or something to that extent, why, then, my application would be unnecessary. But there could be no purpose on the accused's part, and I don't think that he urged otherwise, for his adduction of this material other than to go to show the people in the gully or elsewhere killed in Racak were fighting members of the KLA. That's why he wants this material in, and that's why it is potentially important for the reasons that I've given. Your Honours, if I can return to the theme of the material going to show that material produced by Dragan Jasovic should not be adduced, you have the three statements but can I invite you also to look at Spotlight 16, and with my observations about the police and judicial system generally in mind, can I also explain to Your Honour that in countries where -- it can sometimes be that in countries where police and judicial systems occupy politicised positions, organisations that have the courage to operate according to human rights norms that are acceptable are extremely important sources of information. This one -- and it's more than possible that I will apply to call somebody from this organisation if it's judged appropriate and helpful. This one is headed by Serbs, and you can see from another document that its leader has cited, someone prepared to take grave personal risks in order to preserve standards, you may conclude. If you will be good enough to go to the index, which is the second page, you'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the standing of this document in our debate, though? Because I've written on it, when it was dealt with yesterday, "Nothing established from this document."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what's the status of it for us to consider at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this stage I'm inviting you to consider it entirely de novo as if I'm bringing it to you for the first time on an argument about reliability of Jasovic's material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How can you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a published -- Your Honour, I can and I'd be grateful if I can expand on it even if Your Honour rules against me in due course. This is a document published in February 1995 by an utterly respectable human rights organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So I say. And if you'd be good enough to look, please, at the index, you'll see that 3.3 document of February 1995, page 15, I think it's actually page -- it is page 15, relates to electric shocks at Urosevac police station, and you'll bear in mind that the witness alleged that she'd had no complaints of torture of any kind, and if you look at this well-known publication, what I'm taking you to is but one sample of what is said here was established from 195 people who were interviewed. And at page 3. -- at page 3.3 on page 15, at the foot of page 15 and then over to page 16 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is 1994 you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the relevance of that to the evidence that we were considering yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's the same police station, and it shows, if Your Honour would be good enough to allow me to explain, it shows, apart from recorded systematic use of violence, it shows at the very police station an 18-year-old, and I turn to page 16 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, could you hold on a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll hear from the others on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. On page 16, then, from the same police station in 1994/5, which is, for example, the time of the police trial that the witness did deal with and, more materially, is the same police station as these three people were interviewed at, we see and Your Honours can read it quickly, more quickly than I can read it at acceptable interpretation speed, an account from a young man being beaten and electrocuted at the police station by the police. Now, if that is material, published material, contemporaneous with the events described, or fairly contemporaneous within an overall study that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What year is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1995. And if I can take Your Honours back -- I don't want to read out the gory details of the electrocution -- and incidentally, on the previous page, page 14, there is police brutality at the Urosevac farmer's market, so there is another incident in the same area. If Your Honours would, for speed, be good enough to come back to the cover page or the front page, the centre spoke with 165 persons who claimed to have personal experience with politically or ethnically motivated searches, arrests, or detention. A large majority also described torture or instances of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment during questioning by the Serbian police in Kosovo. In a number of these cases allegations of mistreatment at the hands of the police were confirmed by medical reports signed by ethnic Serb or ethnic Albanian doctors. It was impossible to study all the cases brought to the attention of the centre field researchers. In-depth documentation and analysis were made of only a relatively small proportion of the large number of cases recorded, and so on. So that's the basis of this report. Now, Your Honours, as I say, I'm happy for these purposes to treat it, and indeed should treat it for these purposes, as freestanding material, starting afresh. The Defence offers the tabs 46 and so on into evidence. I'm in a position to say, but here is a contrary statement of three of these witnesses, not only denying the content or the material part of the content of their statement but explaining how the statements were taken by the named officer. I point to you other published material going to show a pattern of violence, including violence and torture at the police station concerned. The Chamber asks itself the question: For the purposes of producing important evidence through hearsay material, can the Chamber be satisfied that there are sufficient indicia of reliability in both the categories that His Honour Judge Bonomy referred to, and my respectful submission would be that it could never conceivably be satisfied as to the important element of reliability, that is to say, the content of the statements for the truth of their contents. And so my request to the Court is to reconsider the production of those exhibits and to rule that they be not admitted. Before turning to our own exhibits and the consequences one way or another for that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pausing there, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What you are asking of us now is to agree with you that the judicial system of Serbia at that time was part of politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to agree with that yet. Of course not. But I am making it quite plain what the Prosecution's position is, which is why it may be necessary, if witnesses like this are called, to explore the matters by all the material available according to the rules of admissibility of this Tribunal. I mention it because there may be in the Chamber an assumption that a judicial or police system is entitled to some credit beyond that to which the evidence may show this one is entitled, and therefore I'm inviting you simply to have in mind our position so that no witness starts with special credit and that there should be no special deference paid to witnesses of the kind we've just seen on account simply of the position that she held, and indeed I asked some opening questions that marked the distinction between, for example, that witness and others named in this case who have been dealt with as people whose evidence could not be accepted in written or other form. Investigators. Investigators that we know about, she was given every opportunity to say anything she liked about them, are unimpeachable, it would appear, by reputation. She has been the subject of many allegations. We only looked at some of them because we didn't have time. The allegations made by lawyers, and I may, if necessary, apply to call one of the lawyers who dealt with the police case. But also other public allegations of an extraordinary kind, if not founded on some accuracy on the part of those reporting to them -- to the people recording them. All I desire is that there should be no special credit given to what is said to be a functioning judicial process or a functioning police service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is still for you to prove.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, respectfully, no. This Chamber has to have and has to develop a real understanding and view of what happened in the former Yugoslavia. And the problem is, and it is a real problem for a Court that can only hear material adduced in the adversarial system, that it may invest institutions in other countries with qualities with which it's familiar from its own experience, and there may be no reason to do that. And I'm simply inviting the Chamber to be careful to establish a level from which it starts to assess the evidence. But Your Honour said it's for me to prove that. Respectfully, no. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The real view, Mr. Nice, that you would want us to have of the judicial system can only be one that is based on evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Precisely so. But when His Honour Judge Kwon says the burden's on me to prove that, I can only prove it through witnesses called to assert the contrary, which is why I took some time, to His Honour Judge Bonomy's disquiet yesterday, in trying to get to the witness who took every opportunity it may be to extend answering, to show allegations of some of those that we have available made against her and supported in part by the material coming from doctors. So that -- I needn't repeat myself. Yes, if it's material to explore this in detail and to establish it in detail, then it has to be done by evidence and I'll go further with that with other witnesses. I've gone some way already. My urging on the Court is not simply to give artificial credit to one institution crediting it with qualities that that institution simply may not have. And I repeat, there is something slightly curious, it may be, in giving credit to, if Chamber was so to do, to a judicial and police system in the former Yugoslavia thus to allow this type of statement in when it has said as against its own investigators -- not its investigators, that would be the accused's characterisation; the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor because they are, in a sense, working for a party so-called, that they're not to be credited with reliability when everything about the creation of this institution and the work of the investigators here shows that they came here to work for and do work for the highest standards of modern humanitarian law and, what's more, are engaged, as everybody else here is, not in prosecuting just one sector of society but looking at investigating and prosecuting all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, Mr. Nice, you're making too much of this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I was responding to His Honour Judge Kwon's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber only acts on the basis of the evidence before it except where presumptions are permissible according to law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was responding to His Honour Judge Kwon's question, and Your Honour's explanation of the position in a sense reinforces my position: There is no presumption of credit -- I can express it in Your Honour's terminology: There is no presumption of credit in favour of material produced by this particular system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Or against.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or against. Neutral. I entirely accept that until evidence is available to show one way or another. So in our -- in our submission, the statements produced reinforced by this version of Spotlight should drive the Chamber to the conclusion that if the accused wishes to rely on the words of the people interviewed, then it's those people who should be called, not by us in our time or in an extended rebuttal case, but by the accused in his time. Your Honour, then can I make the obvious point about the consequences of your decision on this application for material we've adduced or sought to adduce. If the evidence is excluded, then obviously the videos and the interviews produced would not be subject of an application to be produced. It would be unnecessary. If, on the other hand, the Chamber rules against me, and I'm not encouraging that in any sense, I'm just allowing for that possibility because I cannot make this application any more strongly or with any more force and concern than I do, but if it rules against me, then in the same way as the Lituchy counter-statements were allowed in I would invite the Chamber to state that the counter-statements of the three witnesses and indeed the counter-videotapes, which have only be viewed in part but can be viewed in full, should be available to the Chamber for consideration. I can deal with other exhibits --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask a technical question in relation to that. Why did you not try to produce it pursuant Rule 92 bis while you could have done that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You mean over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, we wouldn't have had a legal officer down there who could have taken the statement. If necessary, we can deal with 92 bis later, but we always need a legal officer or a judge down there. These exercises aren't that easy. They take a great deal of organisation, and as it were it's difficult enough to find the people and then to find --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And also there's the question, and we can serve it under 92 bis, and we may do that if it ever becomes necessary, but can I -- Your Honour actually triggers me to think of something else which I've been meaning to say: That the Chamber would also want to have in mind that all this material that the accused has produced through the particular three witnesses but through this last witness has come to our attention at the last possible moment, his intention to rely on it. Now, if we'd had advance notice of detail and so on and so forth, we might have been able to do a great deal more. We might have been able to find those other interviewees who are probably alive, but we couldn't. With future witnesses who may be invited to produce the same material we simply may not have the time or the success that we've had with Andric, Lituchy, and this witness. And indeed with this witness had it not been for the happenchance of the Easter vacation almost certainly we wouldn't have been able to present you with material as valuable for the exercise of judging reliability as we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these the exhibits you say were not included in a Rule 65 ter disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I understand, none of this was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why don't you object to them then?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I drew it to your attention right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, you did but unless you tell us that you object because you'll be prejudiced, then it's difficult to take a firm decision against at least considering the position, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, with great respect, two or three answers to that. I've taken objections along the way. I've made efforts and applications to limit the scope of the accused's evidence. They have all been -- they've been by and large nearly all rejected and I've made it clear that my anxiety is not to limit him by reason of his own amateur status as a litigator; I'm anxious that if material may assist the Chamber and he wants you to see can go in, it should go in. So I have to balance things but I have always tried to draw to your attention this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We had a brief discussion, though, about 65 ter and the absence of material from the disclosure at the stage -- at the beginning of the evidence of a witness. Now, it may not -- was it Gojovic or was it this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It wasn't this witness. It may have been Gojovic, and there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And there was a warning given to the accused at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was a warning that the accused would be kept to the terms of his 65 ter, but of course the 65 ters are so narrow, are so general they pretty well encompass anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. But as far as the material, the exhibits are concerned, they should be disclosed. At least, the existence of the material and the fact that it may be relied upon should have been disclosed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Should have been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Plus the fact that we ought to have had some notification -- it's impossible for us to work without some notification of the detail of what a witness is going to rely on by way of exhibits if he relies on a 65 ter summary as broad as these are, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you might also have in mind that in the Prosecution case the Chamber was fairly lenient in relation to disclosure of exhibits in relation to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two important answers to that question. First, the Chamber was generous in the sense that where documents had not been produced -- had not been identified in our 65 ter list, they were not the subject either of objection by the accused, the amicus, or exclusion by the Chamber, correct. But secondly, the Chamber will recall not only that all exhibits wherever possible were provided in advance but they were regularly provided twice; once generally and then once specifically as long in advance as it was possible for the accused to have once we knew what was going to be relied upon. Of course the general generosity -- I'm not sure it's actually the right word, but the general generosity of approach is one that I've also had in mind in limiting my objections. I simply don't want to be, and I don't want to be seen as somebody who is confining an amateur litigator like this accused by technical provisions, and it's a balance I have to draw between taking that -- that strict position and an overeasy one which perhaps His Honour Judge Bonomy is wondering whether I've taken in relation to these exhibits. But that's what I've been trying throughout to do, and it was with that in mind, just dealing, for example, with the question of general admissibility, that we raised with you, for example, scope of evidence in a few early motions and then explained quite specifically that if you ruled against us, then we would regard that as helpful for our future approach, and it seemed to us that the general drift of the Chamber's rulings was to be inclusive and generous, and that guides me in the approach I take. But nevertheless, it's only by chance that we've been able to lay before you material showing that this evidence is unreliable or doesn't have the indicia of reliability upon which it would be appropriate to rely. Your Honours, I made reference to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The rule -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've had a look at the rule while we've been going on, and it's -- it's rather the other way around. "No evidence shall be admissible if obtained by methods which cast substantial doubt on its reliability or if its admission is antithetical to and would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings." Now, the trouble is that the evidence you submit as indicating the method by which it was obtained casting substantial doubt is not really evidence at the moment. It didn't come in as part of the Prosecution case. It's part of an investigation carried out, and it's -- I have difficult with its status.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, its status as evidence formally may be for ultimately -- for later consideration, but -- and I drew Rule 95 to your attention as one of the overriding Rules of the Tribunal, but the case law rulings, coming from Tadic, I think, on the admissibility of hearsay material all requires generally satisfaction with indicia of reliability. And, of course, if we look at these particular statements, we can also have in mind that one of them on our information, one of the makers of the statement is now dead, so that that would have to satisfy, if produced in the normal and other way, would have to satisfy conditions set out in one of the Rules of the Chamber to which we would have had an opportunity to reply and deal with in detail had we been given notice. Your Honours, I referred to a recent filing dealing with the basis of admissibility of certain Prosecution hearsay material that was relied upon by the assigned counsel in their pleading. I simply draw to your attention that it is, in case anybody wants to discuss it, it is confidential because part of the material referred to in it was, I think, in closed session, but I don't desire to go into it in detail now but it's there for you to consider. Your Honours, that's all I say on my basic submission. Would it be help if I just to turn to the documents we've looked at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is the article by Natasa Kandic, the later article which made an allegation against the last witness. I would invite the Chamber to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are referring to B92.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: B92, yes. I would invite you to say that that is material that by the very fact of its being published in the environment with which you're becoming or are familiar, is material going to the witness's reputation, and although she of course denies it, it's something that you should know exists. As to the next document, it was the petition, we've dealt with that this morning. I'll deal with that with a later witness. We then had a complaint --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm trying to catch up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We then had one -- I think four documents at least relating to Fazli Balaj, the lawyer and his clients, a complaint by him the telegram to the Ministry of the Interior, the complaint by the lawyer to many organs, including the judge and others, about torture, and the ten medical certificates, and I'd invite those to be admitted. The witness dealt with them. The next document was the Spotlight report number 16. Without reference to its value simply as a publicly available document in the previous discussion and for want of time, and I have to observe that this witness was capable of taking a lot of time, I did my best to be fast but limited success, a part of this was put to her, not all of it but I would have done if I had had more time, in particular on page 23 as a public expression of the nature and purpose of the 1994 criminal proceedings over which she either presided or in which she was involved, and this is a public document, it's part of our case on the functioning of the judiciary at that time, and I'd invite the Chamber to admit it for that purpose. I would now also invite the Chamber to admit it for the purpose of showing that there were indeed public complaints of torture, notwithstanding some of the recent answers of the witness where she said no such complaints were known of by her effectively. We then come to the six exhibits, the three videos and the three statements, which I would seek to be admitted on the same grounds as in Lituchy unless the Chamber accedes to my application to exclude all documents bearing the signature of Dragan Jasovic. And then, finally, there is this document which the Chamber will recall, the note by the Prosecutor concerning Racak which was -- it's still not translated. I'm not sure whether it should qualify as a Prosecution or a Defence exhibit. The witness produced it, voluntarily read parts from it, and I simply obliged her to read the full context, but I think one way -- or I respectfully submit, one way or another it ought to be before you as an exhibit. I'm neutral as to on whose account. Your Honours, if I can help you further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No doubt you will wish to exhibit medical reports from Pristina faculty of medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KOWN
utterances.text: There's ten of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's ten of them, yes. I thought I had already mentioned them. If I haven't, it's my oversight. Yes, the ten medical certificates. That is the fourth of the four documents concerning allegations of torture by Isak Aliu, in respect of Isak Aliu. Your Honours, I'm sorry to have taken some time. I gather from Ms. Dicklich that by taking that time I've currently now gone over 50 per cent if we add administrative time to the time I took whereas my own cross-examination was well within the 50 -- well less than the 50 per cent, but there it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may address the points in turn that Mr. Nice has raised, starting firstly with the statements taken by Dragan Jasovic. The Court has or should have in mind at the start that the witness was an investigating judge, as His Honour Judge Bonomy has already stated, and that these documents are part of her court files; documents that were not prepared for this litigation but prepared way back for the purposes of other investigations that came into her hands. The documents, as Your Honours will have seen, had official stamps upon them, and this Tribunal admits hearsay evidence pursuant to the Rules of Evidence in this Court, and therefore in my submission, in our submission, it's clearly an example of evidence that should be admitted and that a professional Bench will then accord weight to in due course. Mr. Nice has referred to Rule 95, and in our submission, there has been no evidence to establish or throw substantial doubt upon the reliability of the statements. It has been material that has been used as ammunition in cross-examination and therefore Rule 95 does not come into play, in our submission, in this instance. There is a clear mechanism for the Prosecution to deal with the statements and the contents of the statements. That mechanism has been referred to on several occasions and can be found in Rule 85(A)(iii), the rebuttal phase of the case. Clearly the Prosecution have to be in a position by the end of the case where they will then decide and take a view on the most important statements and the important witnesses to call during the rebuttal phase, but in our submission, the statements that are produced or, rather, were taken by Dragan Jasovic relate to important evidence on Racak and the presence of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To seek to call.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: To seek to call, yes, Your Honour. To seek to call indeed. They refer to important evidence concerning the presence of the KLA and the incident in Racak, and Your Honours may also have noted that some of the tabs actually precede the Racak event itself. I think tab 48, for example, refers to the 12th of January, 1999. The summary of our points and submissions on this phase of the evidence is that the Court has already made a decision. It was admitted and it is a special example, a special category of court files that have been rightly produced by an investigating judge. Dealing next in turn, if I may, with the three statements that were subsequently taken by the Office of the Prosecution on the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd of April and the three videos that accompany the statements, I'd like to make the following few points: Firstly, that these statements have absolutely no connection to the witness Ms. Marinkovic herself. Unlike the Mr. Lituchy scenario, she did not interview the three -- any of the three men originally or have any connection to the taking of their evidence at that stage and is, therefore, unable to comment upon the substance of their testimony. Again, the statements deal with central allegations, but they constitute classic rebuttal evidence and fall into the same category. As a minor point, it was noted by ourselves that some of the questions in the video clips were in fact clearly leading. One of the questions asked by Mr. Saxon was: "Were you asked or told to touch the wires?" And so we raise that in addition to the points already raised in relation to the way in which parts of the statements may have been taken. So we would seek to argue that these statements are not -- should not be admitted at this stage of the case and should be reserved for the rebuttal stage, an argument which Your Honours have heard on several occasions before. Can I deal briefly with the Spotlight report number 16. As Your Honours have seen, this report was produced by an NGO, the Humanitarian Law Centre, in English and was not produced in the witness's language, and in our submission constitutes a comment on the trial referred to in Defence tab 4. The report is a classic example, we submit, of other people's research and ideas and has no probative value or relevance to this witness's evidence and the Kosovo indictment. It is, importantly, material that was not adopted or spoken to by the witness. She was asked whether the magazine analysis was accurate, and her response to that was to want to go back to the original documents, the indictment and the original source papers. It therefore has no probative value and is in fact potentially dangerous to admit this document which contains comment by an NGO of a particular stance with particular views, and to submit that it should be admitted de novo is, in our submission, inappropriate. There are particular mechanisms for the admission of evidence, and in our submission, this does not fall within any of the categories for it to be entitled to be admitted. Moving on to B92, what appears to be an extract from a website, a website article, this was not produced in the witness's language. In fact, she had said that she had never seen it before, and again, it's written by the head of the NGO Humanitarian Law Centre, Natasa Kandic. The document was used by Mr. Nice to ask the witness about the Fehmi Agani case in which she was not the investigating judge, and she clearly said she had nothing to do with that case. Your Honours will recall that one very serious allegation was put to the witness from the document. In fact, the allegation being that she had ordered several men to be killed. This allegation was not supported by any other material by the Prosecution, and it was denied vehemently, and her presence was denied in relation to the allegation. Again, Your Honours, in our submission, it's the document which falls into the category of contents not adopted by the witness, and importantly, material which includes inappropriate comment by the author about the witness herself. It adds nothing to the witness's evidence that was given in this trial. Understandably, maybe used for ammunition, but nothing beyond that. Your Honours may recall that Mr. Milosevic did re-examine on this document in order to deal with the allegations that were raised by Mr. Nice, and this raises a related point which I would like to bring to Your Honours' attention, that being that when the decisions on the admission of exhibits are left to the end of the testimony of a witness, it does raise problems for the accused, Mr. Milosevic, to know what he has to deal with in re-examination, and we have observed that perhaps an amount of time has been taken up in re-examination which need not have been taken by Mr. Milosevic if an earlier decision about admissibility had been taken at the outset. I make those comments in addition to my comments on admissibility. Your Honours, if I may then briefly deal with the remaining documents. Firstly, the complaint of the defending lawyer and the accompanying telegram and subsequent complaint. Subject to any observations, of course, that Mr. Milosevic may have on the admissibility of this material, we make the following submissions: These documents were presented to the witness and she attempted to deal with them. She addressed them, and they relate to the events referred to in tab 4 of the Defence exhibits. In our submission, it's a category of documents that could be dealt with in terms of weight by the Trial Chamber, bearing in mind, of course, that only partial records have been made available or available to the parties. Similarly, the ten medical examinations fall into the similar category. And finally, dealing with the Prosecution's Official Note concerning Racak that was produced by this witness, there is no objection to that document. It was produced by her and given to the Court. We are concerned by the length of time that has been taken in concern -- with the Prosecution's comments concerning the admissibility of these documents in that it seems to us to be more appropriate that decisions on admissibility of exhibit material be dealt with when they arise so that we avoid the length of time that has perhaps been taken up on these matters, of course important matters but matters which could be perhaps dealt with more swiftly. Your Honour, unless I can be of any further assistance, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. First of all, I wish to say something about a very sweeping, one-sided, even irresponsible, I should say, statement made by Mr. Nice that the judicial system of Yugoslavia was an extended arm of politics. The question is whether the courts ruled according to the law or apart from the law. As you could see in these documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I want you to confine your remarks to the question of the admissibility of the nine documents that we are -- that have been referred to. This is not the occasion to respond to Mr. Nice's remarks about the judicial system.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, Mr. Nice put this forth as a general objection for denying the credibility of the court records and files of the Yugoslav judiciary organs. So that is a question of admissibility, and how. That is why the question is that if we have court records here of judicial organs presented by a witness who is an investigating judge who worked on this, if then there is general -- a general challenge to the judiciary system, then one would have to provide evidence that this judiciary did not function according to the law, which cannot be proven on the basis of these court records. On the contrary; they only prove that the courts did function on the basis of the law. Also, there has to be evidence, then, that the criminal laws and the laws in general in Yugoslavia were not good to begin with and that there are some kind of distorted provisions that do not exist anywhere else in the world. Mr. Nice referred to the trials to -- the trials of illegal police structures. If you establish through the court records that this was a structure that dealt in arms smuggling and murder, and that is what the witness said here, too. I would like Mr. Nice to say where, in which country a Criminal Code does not punish such activities, those that result in murder, arming, et cetera. So he either has to prove that the Criminal Code is simply wrong or that the courts did not work in accordance with the law in order to dare criticise or object to the judicial system in Yugoslavia. Secondly, he says that he is challenging tabs 47, 46, 48, 50, 51, and 54. Always there are two authorised officials on each document, and then Mr. Jasovic appears as one of them. Please, let us just compare two things: Mr. Nice spoke of a test of reliability, and he even said that I did not meet the required criteria when giving this evidence. I believe that the test of reliability has indeed been met, because these are official records of the investigating judge who is giving evidence. Secondly, these are court records that were created on the 16th of January, as is the case in tab 52. Some were created before the 16th of January, and so on. So these are official records that were compiled by authorised officials and official files that are part and parcel of the investigation process conducted by the witness. They were compiled at a time when they could not have had anything to do with the current proceedings here. Mr. Nice confronts this with three statements taken this week which indeed have something to do with this -- these proceedings. They were taken by his co-workers. When you take into account statements that were taken on time and became part of court records and that at that time there were no proceedings like the current ones, and when you take into account, on the other hand, these three statements which do have something to do with these proceedings, and how, because they were taken on account of these proceedings and in order to refute these official records, then it is quite clear that they cannot be considered on a footing of equality at all, because official records are one thing and everything else is another thing. As for the report of this organisation of Mrs. Kandic's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, may I ask you specifically whether you object to the admission of the three statements taken by the Prosecution over the weekend, the Easter weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. This is a malicious procedure, taking statements six years later only for the purposes that can be obvious to anyone. If we -- if we all have to be aware of the situation in Kosovo and Metohija and the terror that reigns there, we would have to know that there is not a single Albanian there any longer who would give you a statement that would be to the detriment of the interests of the KLA. They have killed so many of them that their families do not even dare speak of their next of kin who had been killed. So I'm truly surprised that Mr. Nice dares speak about the reliability of the judicial system of Yugoslavia, and he takes as reliable something that is stated in the darkest days of terror in Kosovo, a terror imposed by the KLA, and everybody knows about that. Many people hear this. This is being telecast. Everybody knows what the situation is like in Kosovo. In that situation these statements are absolutely worthless. I think that it is even not serious to proffer such statements. Secondly, you asked a few minutes ago whether there was any point in showing that these persons were members of the KLA, that there was a KLA presence in Racak. Mr. Robinson, Mr. Kwon, at that time Mr. Bonomy was not here, but you do recall that the witness whose name Mr. Nice mentioned a few minutes ago, Buja Shukri, who was one of the commanders in Racak, here during the cross-examination, he was a Prosecution witness, he himself said that they were the first to open fire at the police from a 12.7-millimetre heavy machine-gun, at the police who were entering Racak. How can there be a question mark concerning the fact that the KLA was in Racak? Well, Shukri himself confirmed this, not to speak of all the other testimonies that are referred to here. So I think it is quite clear that these tabs, that is to say all these statements that Jasovic compiled and that Mrs. Marinkovic as investigating judge included in her records at the time when this was taking place, when it was contemporaneous in 1999, these statements meet even the most rigid criteria of reliability tests, whereas I believe that the statements taken yesterday and the day before yesterday and the conditions under which they are taken and from the persons from which they are taken cannot be acceptable at all. As regards different writings of Mrs. Kandic, let us leave aside the fact that this is propaganda. This is not even hearsay evidence. Quite simply, these are writings about all sorts of things that can compromise the authorities in Yugoslavia, and paper can suffer anything. She even wrote here that Danica Marinkovic, the investigating judge who was testifying here, ordered the police to kill a group of Albanians. And this was even referred to in the cross-examination. Can anyone conceive of such a situation? If such things were to be taken into account as something that merits due consideration, I believe there can be no end to this kind of thing. I'm saying all of this publicly. Everybody can hear this. She -- Natasa Kandic is a highly compromised person in Serbia because of such writings. This therefore has no weight and should not be taken into evidence. After all, General Gojovic, when he was confronted with a similar thing, he suggested to you that if you care about your own credibility, you should not be dealing with Mrs. Kandic. Furthermore, Mr. Nice said that there was much abuse, once again referring to the Spotlight writings, and so on and so forth. Gentlemen, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you here had the opportunity of seeing that, and in this specific case it was Judge Marinkovic but it can happen to any investigating judge, did have an opportunity of getting a complaint from one of the Defence counsel of one of the accused and that she issued orders that a medical examination be conducted. Now, if what Mr. Nice said were true in the 1990s, and he mentioned 1994 and 1995 about some instances of torture, then the following question arises: How come that at that time -- it was peace at the time, there was no, no extraordinary situations in Kosovo and Metohija at the time, how come then, given that situation in the towns in which this happened, nobody filed criminal reports about having been abused by the police, that they had overstepped their authority, and so on and so forth? Perhaps there are reports of that kind. I don't know that there is a single police force in the world where individuals do not overstep their mark, especially in situations of crisis. But if we're talking about torture and abuse, how come these people did not file criminal reports to the authorities telling them that such-and-such had happened, when we have on the other side an example whereby criminal reports were filed on the basis of which Danica Marinkovic made certain decisions and so on and took certain steps. And Mr. Nice said that even medical material confirm assertions about the judiciary. Medical reports confirm quite the opposite assertions, and that is what Mrs. Marinkovic said. She said as soon as a complaint or request came in from a Defence counsel, it would be her -- she herself who would order that a medical examination be conducted, which shows precisely that she was working according to the letter of the law and working according to the professionalism of a judge. And he used an expression, he said, "You have ten reports on torture." So he uses those terms and creates an atmosphere who, for the layman, might appear to be the truth. So those ten reports on torture - I haven't counted them all, but anyway in nine of them it says that what was found was light bodily injury and that in one case no injuries were found at all. Therefore what right has Mr. Nice to speak about ten reports about torture or this I don't know. I should like the public to assess this and it is up to you to assess this. I have seen no ten reports on torture, although he brought that up and used it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, no jury.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is. There is indeed, Mr. Robinson. There is a jury. Yes, there is. The jury is the entire world public. And the advantage of the 21st century is that nothing can be hidden. And finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is a public trial, but when I say there is no jury, I was really responding to your remarks about a particular purpose behind Mr. Nice's presentation of his case, as if that were to impress a layman. There is no layman here as the trier of facts. We are professional Judges. It is for that reason that I reminded you that there is no jury here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, it is not my intention to undermine your professional knowledge, and I do not think that Mr. Nice had the impression -- had the intent to impress you, because you have seen the documents and they're not documents about torture, you can see that for themselves. But he does have the intention of impressing the public because we are talking about a propaganda war here that is still ongoing and has been ongoing for the last 15 years. And part of that is the activities of Mr. Nice with qualifications that he makes and which cannot be supported. Secondly, Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We now know that you have an intention to impress the public. Will you be terminating your comments shortly, Mr. Milosevic, because we are well past the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will, Mr. Robinson. I don't want to underestimate your powers of perception, but since you have said that Mr. Nice wanted to impress the public, then I would have to reassess my assessment of your capabilities of noticing things, if I can put it that way. Mr. Nice very often refers to witness statements, the statements of witnesses, and you can find people like that in their thousands in Kosovo and Metohija who will be ready to say that I came by at night to slaughter people. Gentlemen, they are witnesses who, despite the material facts which we were able to see and had in evidence, how many dead people after the NATO bombings in the centre of Pristina, the columns of refugees, and a series of other things, claim that they had nothing against it, that they had absolutely nothing against it. It didn't affect them. The only thing they were doing was fleeing from Serb forces. Now, if you have material facts and assertions of that kind, then you yourselves and the public at large can assess what kind of witnesses they have before them. So I consider that this evidence provided by Mr. Nice should not be accepted. I agree that the notes of the Prosecutor with respect to Racak ought to be included because they are court files and speak of what the prosecutor did. And with that, I have completed what I wanted to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Six sentences, with Your Honours' leave. There is no explanation given by either Ms. Higgins or the accused as to why important witnesses of this kind haven't been called in person -- important people of this kind haven't been called to give evidence. The preference for indirect testimony on important issues is not explained. The point that the material of the accused has already been admitted made by Ms. Higgins must be met in this way: When I'm presented with material so late, I cannot know what position to take. I work as hard as I can to establish what position I should take. I don't take positions, as I explained earlier, without having a reason to do so. Thus I simply can't. If he brings an exhibit in now and I know that you're likely to admit it because it falls in a certain category of document, I can't say it is unreliable without some cause for saying that. Lituchy, the suggestion is that this witness, unlike Lituchy, is unable to comment. Yes. On her evidence. Thus I'm simply unable to cross-examine the material in any way. Where has the adversarial system, with which we are obliged to work gone? I cannot meet the evidence, I cannot deal with it. The Agani allegation was put very carefully by me, my duty to put, especially if I intend to call evidence on it later or seek to do so, and I put it in terms of could she think of any reason why police officers would make those allegations about her? The suggestion of calling the evidence in rebuttal was topsy-turvy. Important evidence that could have been called by this accused by calling the witnesses, completely topsy-turvy, non-adversarial world. Shukri Buja, yes, the Prosecution called evidence about the activities of the KLA in order to give the Court a full account. Mrs. Kandic, the accused went through this document - I'm grateful for Ms. Higgins reminding me of this - in great detail. That's the short document from B92. The Court may care, if it finds it helpful, to see the risks she personally has to take in what is a dangerous environment. Finally, before I come to two other observations, light bodily injury, I've dealt with that. The allegation against the witness was quite clear. Light bodily injury only showed because she had intentionally delayed the examination process. As His Honour Judge Bonomy observed it was a blunt instrument injury. In general, the accused could have been calling the policeman who led the attack or whatever it was at Racak. Popovic, identified as the military person who explained to Maisonneuve that the army shelled Racak. Radosavljevic, the man who on the videotape says in terms he went in in a joint operation with other forces. He doesn't. He calls this evidence and hopes to get it by you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a correction. I don't remember Mr Popovic said. The army shelled Racak. It is MUP with Praga and tank support.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right, it's Praga and tank support, but that -- well, I'll have another look at it, but in any event, I'm grateful for that. The accused acknowledges in terms that he's using this court to speak to a worldwide jury. I'm sure that Your Honour's observation about my intentions were in order to lighten the atmosphere the accused was creating, but let it be quite clear I not only am concerned to keep the atmosphere of this court as calm as it may be, and that's one of the reasons I'm as non-interventionist as I have been, but I have drawn to the Court's attention the very real concerns that there are for the region about the use of the public access this accused has, and of course I have absolutely no intention or desire of impressing the public in the way that the accused suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, why is it that the argument you've advanced doesn't apply to Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It always could have been raised. Maisonneuve was provided -- if it was said that this was unreliable -- Your Honour is quite right, I don't challenge the source of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Surely you'd do the same as you accuse Ms. Higgins of, turning it topsy-turvy by saying the accused could call Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He could call Popovic now because Popovic is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's an accident of the order in which the case is presented. It's no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but if Your Honour is referring to the fact that evidence was given of what an involved person said, it would always have been open - and this is the way the procedure works - for the amicus, as Mr. Kay then was, or for the accused to say, well, this is an important piece of evidence and its reliability is not established, therefore, please exclude it. Nothing to stop them doing that. That they didn't do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And for the record, I have to make a correction. It was K6 who referred to Petrovic, not Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Petrovic. Yes. I'm sorry. Your Honour, thank you very much for the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. Please, before we adjourn, in the interests of time, the liaison officer informed me that with this possible witness Jasovic, that she can come into contact with him only after 2.00 p.m. and that she'll do her best to make an appointment for him to see me tomorrow afternoon. That is why I should like to ask you to issue orders to give me the transcripts from yesterday's and today's testimony of Mr. Jasovic for me to have a look in order to prepare. I'll just need an hour with him tomorrow afternoon at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'd better tell the Court that some of his evidence is in closed session, and we're drafting something to try and deal with it today and get an application in before the other Trial Chamber for release of those transcripts that are in closed session and any exhibits and other materials there may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is for that Trial Chamber to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, under the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it is for that Trial Chamber, not this one, to order the disclosure of that testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He's still currently giving evidence as well and is being cross-examined by one of the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: His public session can be accessible to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, we heard your submissions on that point. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Milosevic, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Professor Dobricanin.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, tell us, please, where and when you were born.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: I was born on the 10th of December, 1937, in Prokuplje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where did you live and where do you reside now?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: From 1953 to 1999, I lived in Pristina. I am now temporarily residing in Krusevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did you leave Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: On the 26th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what education have you had?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: I graduated from the faculty of medicine. Labour medicine was my specialisation, and forensic medicine. So that is my education. I have a Ph.D., a doctorate in medicine. Otherwise, I'm a doctor of science, and I am regular professor teaching forensic medicine at the faculty of Pristina, temporarily residing in Kosovska Mitrovica, or, rather, the faculty is located in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are also an author of textbooks in forensic medicine for students studying the subject?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Professor, where have you worked, briefly, your CV?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: From December 1965, having completed my military training, I worked at the infirmary for labour medicine and the Elektroprivreda Kosovo firm. I worked there until 1973 when, at the invitation of the state organs, I moved to work in the field of crime technology in the laboratory for forensics of the then-Secretariat for Internal Affairs in Pristina, and at the same time, I was the head of the health service. And in 1983, after receiving a Ph.D. and everything that came to pass afterwards, I started working at the faculty and the Institute for Forensic Medicine. From 1973 until 1972 [as interpreted], I was assistant professor at that same faculty, although I also worked in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When were you elected full professor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: I was elected full professor in 19 -- I'll tell you exactly, just a moment. In 1987 or 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. The key topic of your testimony has to do with the events in Racak, and the date is from the 15th of January, 1999. And in this list against me, in paragraph 66(A), is described in the following way, I'm going to read it out to you: "On the 15th of January, 1999 -- on or about the 15th of January, 1999, the village of Racak (Stimlje municipality) was attacked by forces the FRY and Serbia. After shelling, the forces of the FRY and Serbia entered the village later in the morning and began conducting house-to-house searches. Villagers who attempted to flee from the forces of the FRY and Serbia were shot throughout the village. A group of approximately 25 men attempted to hide in a building but were discovered by the forces of the FRY and the police. They were beaten and then they were removed to a nearby hill where they were shot and killed. Although the forces of the FRY and Serbia killed approximately 45 Kosovo Albanians in and around Racak --" "altogether" the word was to begin with, not "although," and then it goes on to say that those persons killed who are known by name are set forth in Schedule A which is attached as an appendix to this indictment. Professor, I'm going to ask you very concrete questions, but before we go on to my questions can you tell me whether what I have just read is true, on the basis of everything that you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, where were you and what were you doing when the event of Racak took place on the 15th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: I was working at the institute with my colleagues. I was working on autopsies because there were a lot of civilians and policemen who had lost their lives, and soldiers, due to the bombing and the activities of the terrorist KLA, so we had a large number of corpses to deal with every day. So we had to do post-mortem examinations from early morning until night. We were very busy with this work at the Institute of Forensic Medicine when the information arrived that we had to go on the spot to Racak because something had happened there, some fighting or something I didn't know anything about specifically, but I prepared to go on site to conduct an examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did you set out for the village of Racak for the first time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: On the 7th [as interpreted] of January, 1999. I think it was sometime around 7.00 in the morning, perhaps a little earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, how did it come about that you went to the village? Who called you and why?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: I was called by Mrs. Danica Marinkovic, the investigating judge of the district court in Pristina. She asked me to go with her and the deputy prosecutor and the crime technician to carry out an on-site examination in the village of Racak where, according to certain information which had not been checked out until then, about 40 to 45 Kosovo Albanians had been killed in fighting, in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, did you happen to go to on-site examinations when asked to do so by the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Yes, very frequently.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down and make pauses between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic and Professor, the interpreters are asking you to slow down so that they can follow you. Observe a pause between the question and the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, who else in addition to Judge Danica Marinkovic and yourself went off to conduct an on-site examination to Racak?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: The deputy district prosecutor. His name was Dragan Zivic, and the scene-of-crime officer went with us, men who are accustomed to carry out scene of crime investigations, as well as the policemen who provided security for us and escorted us. I don't think there was anyone else up until Urosevac, whereas in Racak, when everything ended, the observers went with us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where did you arrive first en route to Racak?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: We arrived at the police station in Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say you arrived at the police station in Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. And who received you there at the police station?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: The police station we were received by the head of the SUP, chief of SUP in Urosevac. Bobi Janicijevic was his name. I don't know his first name. He was called Bobi Janicijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. So you were received by the chief of the Urosevac SUP, his surname was Janicijevic. Now, tell me, did he -- you receive any information as to what had happened in Racak from him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Well, all he said to me and the investigating judge and the others was that on the 15th of January there was fighting in Racak between the police forces and members of the KLA, and that in that fighting approximately 40 - they didn't have an exact figure at that time - that 40 members of those terrorist forces had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did Mr. Janicijevic tell you anything about the situation in Racak and the surrounding area before this event came to pass, this event of the 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Well, I knew myself that next to Racak and along the road running near Racak, that you couldn't pass by that way, and that had been the situation for several months, because the communication lines towards Suva Reka and Prizren and Urosevac and the road running from Pristina to Skopje, well, were held under fire and was often attacked, civilians passing by in their own cars were often under attack. So that quite simply we ceased to travel that way. When the need arose for us to do any post-mortems or go to the Court in Prizren, we had to use another route. And we were cautioned of this situation by Mr. Janicijevic, who told us that it was from that village and from the hills around the village that there was frequent shooting and that people or, rather, policemen were frequently killed and wounded in that locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did Mr. Janicijevic tell you anything about the immediate cause or pretext for the police operation in Racak on the 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: The immediate pretext or cause was the killing of two policemen and attacks on the police force in that general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what, according to Mr. Janicijevic was the object of that police operation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: The object of that police operation was to repel from the village the terrorists who had come in there from different locations. According to his statement and the statement of others, that was a centre of a terrorist unit, a terrorist unit of the KLA. And it was the assignment of the police force to repel them back across the hills to the mountains and lakes, Klecka and all that general region. And quite simply that the headquarters that had existed there to be done away with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did he tell you anything about the fact that the army had taken part? Did they mention the army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: No. To the best of my knowledge, the army had not taken part in this operation. He said it was exclusively a police operation without any army there, any soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about you yourself? Did you have anything to go by and to conclude whether the army took part in this operation or not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: I didn't see a single soldier, nor did anybody enter that area generally, or no army vehicles either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, since you're a forensic expert, if the army had taken part, would there have been army officials there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Yes. The military investigation organs would have been there and my colleagues from the medical military academy would have taken part in the autopsies for Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Janicijevic describe the actual events that took place in Racak?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: In the briefest of terms. He told me and Mrs. Danica Marinkovic what he could. He -- I wasn't interested in the details but what he did say was that it was an operation that started in the early hours of the morning and that there was heavy fighting and that members of the KLA had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did he tell you about the casualties in that event?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: He said that they were members of the terrorist KLA organisation which had been troubling them and causing great problems in the village and in the surrounding areas, in other villages close by, close to Racak, and that they had to launch this operation to deblock the roads and the communication lines and to prevent future terrorist operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about the weapons they had seized during the operation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Before we arrived in Stimlje, when we went to SUP - and that was the 17th of January - it was the SUP of Urosevac, in actual fact, I saw the weapons there in a room. There were a lot of automatic rifles, Kalashnikovs, and so on. There was a 12.7-millimetre machine-gun. I know the calibres very well, it's part of my job and profession. And then Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there was a Browning too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, before this event, in view of the fact that you were always involved in medical examinations of the deceased in your institute, do you know how many KLA were present in the area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Everything I'm saying is based on the policemen's stories when they brought in the corpses, and I learnt that that was an area, there was a feature that was dominant, an elevation between Drenica and Jezerska Planina of Klecka, the mountains there, and other villages in the area, that was a stronghold of the terrorist organisation and that there had been severe fighting there before and that they had tried to repel them from the area, however it was very difficult and a large number of policemen were killed from Drenica and along that general mountain ridge in the proximity of those villages and Jezerska Planina next to Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you meet anybody else at the police station in Stimlje?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: At the police station in Stimlje, some ten minutes after our arrival, a general entered. He introduced himself as being the British general, John Drewienkiewicz was his name, with an interpreter, or two interpreters, I assume, or one might have been an interpreter and another young lady was there, I don't know in what capacity, but he introduced himself. He said, "I am the famous General John Drewienkiewicz," although I'd never heard of him before. He was very arrogant in his conduct towards us at that time, and I have very unfavourable memories when he started issuing orders and telling us that we couldn't go to Stimlje and that in Stimlje the only people that could go to Stimlje was the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean Stimlje or Racak?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: I mean Racak. I apologise. I mean Racak. That we couldn't go into Racak and the only people that could accompany the investigating judge was I myself, possibly, without an armed escort and that he couldn't guarantee security, but that if anybody were to shoot at the inhabitants of the village of Racak, he would personally take Mrs. Danica Marinkovic to The Hague. And then she asked him, "And what will happen, General, if they should happen to shoot at us?" And his answer was, "The same will happen because you provoked them, and I will take you and detain you and take you to The Hague in that case too." After hearing those words, Mrs. Danica Marinkovic stopped talking to him and ordered us to set off towards the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. He told you thus that you couldn't go to Racak.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The investigating judge decided to go to Racak nevertheless. Do you know why the investigating judge decided that way?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: In addition to the threats that he issued at the office in the police station in Stimlje, this same gentleman, Mr. Drewienkiewicz, told us when we left the office and when we were setting off to Racak that the -- we couldn't go, but the investigative judge felt that she was the only one who was competent to go and who was authorised to go, and moreover, required to go under the legislation of Kosovo and Metohija and the Republic of Serbia. So she acted in accordance with the law that prevailed in our country, and I believe she was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
