utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. How many people and how many vehicles did you have in that group that set off to Racak?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: There was investigative Judge Marinkovic, leader of that group, deputy district Prosecutor Dragan Zivic, I as a doctor. There were scene of crime officers, I don't know how many. I remember that one of them even had a camera, a video camera. There were many policemen who were guarding us. We took several police vehicles of the Pinzgauer type, I believe they're called, and we set off in a motorcade. We passed by a hospital or a hospice for handicapped persons, taking a village road, and as we came close, we could see the mosque. I knew it was a mosque, it was clearly marked, and that's where we stopped awaiting further information as to the security situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what happened? Did you establish that it was safe to go on?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: I personally saw in Racak that there was life, there were people, that it was not completely vacant. Around the mosque there were some men and women moving, although I must say I have very vague memories of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From what distance, Professor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: It could have been 700, 800 metres, perhaps a little more. At one point volleys of automatic fire came down upon us, and we bent down behind our cars. That was the only shelter we could find. It seemed to come from everywhere at the same time. I couldn't estimate where it was coming from exactly. And after awhile, when the fire died down a little, when it abated and when the security situation stabilised a little, we agreed that we should go back to Stimlje because there were no proper conditions to conduct an on-site investigation, so that's what we did. We returned to Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was it for the day. Which day was that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: The 17th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did you finally manage to get to Racak? When was your next attempt to go to Stimlje and Racak?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: I went to Stimlje on the next day, the 18th of January, around 10.00. That was the day when this whole story with General Drewienkiewicz took place. It didn't happen the first time, on the 17th, but on the 18th, and it is on the 18th that what I just described happened. Sometime around 10.00, after talking to General Drewienkiewicz, we set off - it was by that time 11.00, I believe - towards Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of police escort did you have?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: We had a police escort including several cars, some of them armoured. We personally travelled in a Lada Niva vehicle which had only one windshield in the back that was armoured. And when we finally arrived at Racak, there was nobody, nobody there to be seen unless they were hiding in their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when you arrived at the village, there was no one.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there anything to indicate that the village had been shelled? Because you remember what it said in that paragraph of the indictment that I quoted.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: No, there was no sign whatsoever that there had been shelling. There was not a single house that was damaged, at least from what I was able to see, and I toured a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where in Racak did you find corpses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: We had previously received information that morning that there were bodies in the mosque in Racak. And when we entered the village of Racak, we turned left, as far as I can remember. We came to the same mosque that I had seen the previous day. We saw the vehicles of OSC observers, orange vehicles. So when we arrived there, we talked to OSC observers. Our escorts and the scene-of-crime officers entered the mosque. There was a police officer who was standing in the middle of the mosque. Inside the mosque, our scene of crime officers had already started marking the places where the bodies were lying. The bodies were lined along the walls of the mosque, and there was a line of bodies in the middle of the mosque. All the bodies were clothed. Some did not have any shoes. Some faces were covered by kerchiefs, some were covered by Albanian flags. I came up to a body that was the first in the row next to me to see what kind of injuries it presented, and it happened to be a person whose head had been completely destroyed. Fragments of the skull were lying nearby, next to the body. I covered the body. I toured the mosque to see all the bodies to see if there were any injuries that could have been sustained immediately after death. I didn't notice anything of the kind. On one body I saw an incision in the stomach. I didn't look any more. I indicated to Judge Marinkovic that they should be transported to the Institute of Forensic Medicine, and she gave appropriate orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How were they dressed, those people who had been killed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: On the spot and later, the Institute of Forensic Medicine, when we performed post-mortems, we saw the bodies were dressed in dark coloured clothing; black, navy blue, dark brown, and that was not surprising. I'll explain why. In all the work that I performed in those years on the ground and at the institute, I worked with a lot of bodies of casualties of the conflict which had not been called war at the time, and I know that they wore green clothing and dark clothing -- dark clothing. That was the usual clothing worn by units of people who were self-organised to guard their villages. I have my information from lots of people who brought in these bodies. Those are some facts that I was able to ascertain, among other things, while performing my post-mortems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just one thing. You said that the upper part of the body was dressed in black, navy blue, dark brown. You're not talking about uniforms, are you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: No. The only thing that was specific to Racak, lots of them wore heavy boots wearing the mark Ozel, two dots above the O. Some of them had belts that looked like military belts. And on the bodies with which I worked at the institute, we found, although very rarely, some uniforms marked KLA, and what was very interesting was that not everybody had emblems and insignia. Some had something on the cap or on the sleeve or on the breast pocket, and it was only in Malisevo that we found bodies dressed in complete uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say you found a total of four bodies dressed in uniform in your entire time there, that means that that was the total of bodies wearing KLA uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that the other bodies did not have uniforms on them.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, you mentioned that some bodies were covered by Albanian flags and some were not. Why did you emphasise that? Does that have any significance in view of your experience and knowledge about these things or did you mention it just by the way?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: It does have significance. Even before the conflict, on all the persons who died in Kosovo, Metohija as fighters, their bodies would be found covered by Albanian flags. Sometimes just the head, but usually the entire body. It was an honour given to them as people who had died for the freedom of Kosovo. This was just an indication, because in this case, in the case of Racak, there was only three or four flags, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you did not examine the bodies immediately apart from uncovering a couple of bodies before covering them again to view them in greater detail at the Institute of Forensic Medicine.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How long was your on-site examination, if I can call it that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Ten to 15 minutes, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to make any conclusions during that first immediate examination or viewing, although I do bear in mind that it was a very short time and a very superficial examination. Were you able to conclude anything about the cause of death of these persons?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: The cuts in the clothing that I noticed - and I have great experience with this - told me that the injuries were caused by gunfire, gunshots mainly in the head, in the chest and the abdomen, and that great damage was done to internal organs and the brain. This was the sort of blitz examination, the conclusions of which were later confirmed by post-mortems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from concluding that these persons were shot, were you able to conclude something about the distance from which it was fired or the direction from which it was fired at the bodies?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: No, not at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the condition of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: In view of the low temperatures that prevailed during those few days, and I have to say the bodies were found four days later, they were quite well preserved from what I could see, and I was able to observe faces, hands and feet. The smell was not too strong and decomposition had not gone very far. And later when we transported them to Pristina, to the institute, we indeed were able to see that they were rather well preserved, better than if they had been kept in some other conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you take longer for this examination?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: We had been delayed by this talk with Mr. Drewienkiewicz. We were delayed from the start. It was getting dark, and we knew that after arriving, we should not linger because the way back was going to be difficult, too, and the roads to Stimlje and further on was difficult as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about the identification of these persons on the spot?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: There were some comments that I could hear, but I didn't pay too much attention. Some people saying that some bodies were already identified and that some of them belonged to earlier -- people earlier identified as KLA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were OSCE observers present?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Yes, they were with us all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there journalists as well?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Yes. There were two of them, and there was a camera there as well. I don't know who was filming and for whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that all the bodies were numbered by scene-of-crime officers. Were they also photographed on the spot in the mosque?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Yes. They were photographed, and they were numbered 1 to 40. It was done on the spot by scene-of-crime officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was then done with the bodies?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic issued orders that the bodies be loaded on the truck and transported to the Institute of Forensic Medicine. We set off through the village, through those narrow streets where the fighting had taken place according to our information, and when we came close to the trenches, we heard explosions from mortar shells, I suppose. It was something very powerful. And the policeman who accompanied us found out that the truck with the bodies was fired at from mortars in an attempt to destroy the truck and the bodies in it. However, the truck driver very skilfully avoided this fire and continued his way to Stimlje, which is very close, as I said earlier. We did not attach any particular importance or significance to this at the time while we were touring the trenches. We were just surprised. We couldn't understand. We couldn't think of any reason why anybody would fire at the truck. It was a pretty unique situation where we had to fight to preserve the bodies instead of preserving life, and it was a true fight for the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the bodies were transported on a truck. Who loaded the bodies onto the truck?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: The policemen who were present. They were the only people who could be used for doing that work. There was no one else there. The crime scene officers accompanied us when we transported the bodies to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Professor. Tell me, on the basis of your later findings, once you carried out the autopsies, could you conclude that while the bodies were not under your supervision somebody had affected their state in some way?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: There were no visible signs of any kind of body removal. I don't know. If I were on the scene immediately on the 15th, we could have had a lot more information, and we could speak with a great deal more certainty as to whether the bodies had been manipulated. However, we did find something which was very important and which showed that for quite awhile the bodies had been outdoors. We found the traces of teeth of various rodents, starting with rats and then even foxes. And also of some bigger bodies, perhaps -- bigger animals. Perhaps it was wild dogs or wolves or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Where did you go when you left Racak?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: I accompanied Mrs. Marinkovic, the investigating judge, who went to a house right below the hills where we found the trenches later. We entered the premises. I saw a great many scattered things there belonging to KLA members. They took pictures with weapons. I saw an Albanian flag and also documents, lists scattered about. I really was not very interested in this. I was just interested in seeing what headquarters looked like under such circumstances. However, I went out and I looked at some of the smaller rooms on the side next to the headquarters. I found a mess hall, a dining hall with a long table and dishes that were used for serving food. I found a kitchen and white coats that were probably used by cooks and the like. Then I found a warehouse where there were many packages coloured -- that were yellow, and it said "US Aid" on them or something like that. And those were packages that we found everywhere in Kosovo when the police would seize something, when there would be some fighting. And sometimes in the pockets of participants in the conflicts we would find such packages. There were quite a few packages there. We also found some sacks with flour, sugar. In the upper part of the yard there was a bakery that could be seen from the distance. And also there were some buildings, but I don't know what their purpose was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Professor. You described to us now, let's just dwell on this for a few moments, that you saw a dining-room. It was some kind of a room for collective meals, if I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said there was a long table and benches.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For how many people was this, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Well, to give a rough approximation now, there were two benches, one on each side. Perhaps 30 or 40 people. Say about 30 people could sit down and have lunch there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What you saw there, that is to say headquarters and these materials, you saw the dining-room or, rather, a mess hall, then cooks' clothing, warehouses with food. Did this look like a type of barracks to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: Since I had completed my military service and since I was a reserve officer, that's exactly what it looked like to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you go afterwards from these KLA headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA DOBRICANIN
utterances.text: We went to the left side of the village a couple of hundred metres and we came across a bunker -- I'm sorry, a trench, rather, that had been dug in the soil that actually had a lot of sand and rocks in it. Then there was a path going upwards, bending a bit to the left and then coming back in the form of a horseshoe towards the mid part of that ridge. We saw there an area that was covered with these sacks, and underneath there were some wooden boards. This looked like a bunker. Right next to the place we saw a hole that had been dug, perhaps about one metre 20, 30 centimetres deep, and then it was about two metres wide. I saw in that hole a lot of casings, 12.7 millimetres. I again stress this ammunition, I saw it many times due to my own professional work. And there was also a kind of wooden tripod. That's what it looked like. Since I saw that machine-gun at Urosevac on the previous day, this was actually an auxiliary tripod for the Browning 12.7-millimetre machine-gun. I can say that from that spot the entire village of Racak can be seen out in the open. The communication -- rather, the road that goes to Racak and to the centre of Stimlje, rather, part of the road going towards Crnoljev and then via Suva Reka to Prizren. Also, a long part of the road from Pristina to Skopje, and part of the old road which is between Stimlje and Urosevac. So this is a dominant feature that was exceptionally good for someone who would want to follow all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we'll have to stop today. Professor, it's the end of the day's proceedings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask a question before we adjourn? Doctor, my understanding is that you are a medical doctor, a medical expert. Do you have also an expert --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- knowledge in military weapons? So can you really identify an auxiliary tripod for the Browning 12.7-millimetres machine-gun or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely yes, Your Honour Judge Kwon. I've been doing this kind of work for 30 years. I worked in the technical service and there was a ballistics lab within it, and I always worked on these ballistic problems when murders were committed by a certain weapon. We would even try to ascertain the distance, and we did whatever else it took in order to identify the weapons concerned. I am rather well-versed as far as weapons are concerned generally speaking. I used to be a good hunter myself and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
